docs.title: PyTexas Runbooks
docs.text:
This site contains various runbooks and materials detailing how the PyTexas Foundation runs various events, from meetups to conferences.

The material on this site is available for everyone to use in organizing their own events. We are constantly revising the material of this site, so it should always be considered a "Work in Progress" site.

docs.title: Welcome to the PyTexas Conference Documentation
docs.text:
This site is built on mkdocs and uses the mkdocs-material theme.

We welcome contributions, however, since these are the runbooks used for executing PyTexas, we reserve the right to reject PRs on the premise that it is not how we do things.

If you are starting your own conference and want to use this as a baseline for your operations feel free to fork!

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This project uses modern Python tooling for development. You'll need to install:

  1. uv - Fast Python package manager
    • Install: curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
    • More info: uv documentation
  2. just - Command runner for project tasks
    • Install: cargo install just or brew install just
    • More info: just documentation
  3. lychee (optional) - Link checker for documentation
    • Install: cargo install lychee or brew install lychee
    • More info: lychee documentation
    • If you don't install this, the CI will catch any broken links and fail the build.

docs.title: Developing Locally
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository and install dependencies:

    git clone https://github.com/pytexas/runbooks.git
cd runbooks
just install  # or: uv sync

  2. Start the development server with hot reload:

    just serve  # or: uv run mkdocs serve

    The site will be available at http://localhost:8000

  3. Build the static site:

    just build  # or: uv run mkdocs build

docs.text:
Run just help to see all available commands:

  • just serve - Start development server
  • just build - Build static site
  • just validate - Build with strict validation
  • just link-check - Check all links
  • just check - Run all quality checks
  • just clean - Clean generated files

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: To organize a weekly online coffee meetup for PyTexas pythonistas to supplement the existing monthly meetup on Discord.

docs.title: Identify Key Details
docs.text:
• Frequency: Weekly
  • Day & Time: [e.g., Every Saturday at 10 AM]
  • Duration: 1-2 hours
  • Platform: Discord (using the existing server)

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Channels:
  • Create a dedicated voice channel for the meetup.
  • Optionally, create a text channel for discussions and resource sharing.
  • Permissions:
  • Ensure the channels have the appropriate permissions set for participants.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
• Announcement:
  • Announce the meetup details on the Discord server and other communication channels (e.g., email, social media).
  • Reminders:
  • Send a reminder 2-3 days before the meetup.
  • Send a final reminder on the day of the meetup.

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text:
• Welcome & Introduction: (10 minutes)
  • Welcome attendees
  • Introduce new members
  • Discussion Topics: (30-40 minutes)
  • Open discussion on Python-related topics
  • Share experiences, projects, and challenges
  • Networking: (30-40 minutes)
  • Informal networking
  • Encourage attendees to mingle and connect in breakout rooms (if available) or through structured questions.
  • Closing: (10 minutes)
  • Summarize key points discussed
  • Announce the next meetup details

docs.title: Logistics
docs.text:
• RSVP System:
  • Use a tool like Meetup.com, Eventbrite, or a Google Form for RSVPs to estimate attendance.
  • Materials:
  • Prepare any discussion prompts or topics in advance.
  • Have a list of icebreaker questions ready to facilitate conversation.
  • Feedback:
  • Collect feedback after each meetup to improve future sessions (use a simple Google Form or Discord poll).

docs.title: Post-Meetup
docs.text:
• Follow-Up:
  • Share a summary of the meetup on Discord and other channels.
  • Highlight key discussions and any resources shared.
  • Next Meetup Planning:
  • Update the details for the next meetup based on feedback and attendance.

docs.title: Community Chair
docs.text: The Community Chair leads the Community Committee: community outreach, Discord and the custom bot, streaming operations, the virtual experience, and attendee communications and aftercare.

docs.title: Pre-Event
docs.text:
• Run community outreach to the four Texas metro meetups (Austin, DFW, Houston, San Antonio) and coordinate meetup announcements with Marketing.
  • Maintain the Discord server and the custom registration bot (hosted on DigitalOcean). Develop the bot like software: PR-reviewed, demoed in meetings, slash commands scoped to what is realistic by conference time (/poll, /question, /schedule first).
  • Keep a second maintainer on the bot's registration integration; the bot fails for bulk corporate purchases (registering email vs attendee email), so have a manual fallback.
  • Plan streaming operations on YouTube: test stream at least one week ahead, and train at least one backup on the full streaming and chat workflow. A solo streaming operator is a single point of failure if they get sick.
  • Design the virtual experience: private attendee chat channel, engagement ideas (coding puzzles, setup photo thread, trivia and polls), and clear ticket messaging that states which days each ticket covers. Attendees without tutorial tickets show up Friday when the site only says a three-day range.
  • Capture speaker Discord handles at intake so day-of Q&A follow-up works.
  • Recruit walk leaders for the organizer-led group lunches and any extras (e.g. a nature walk).
  • Build the signage map on the Miro board with Venue.

docs.title: Day of Event
docs.text:
• Run the YouTube stream: go live 10-15 minutes early each day.
  • Moderate Discord chat; post speaker links and socials live as talks progress, and route overflow Q&A to speakers in the channel.
  • Compile every link shared in the conference-chat channel into one doc during the event, organized by day.
  • Run the virtual engagement program and answer virtual attendee questions.
  • Stick to one chat tool for day-of coordination; monitoring several chat tools at once does not work.

docs.title: Post Event
docs.text:
• Send attendee aftercare communications and promote the post-event survey with Marketing.
  • Finish the link-compilation doc and file it in the year's Drive folder.
  • Get recordings onto pyvideo.org via a manual pull request to the pyvideo/data repo; this is a single-volunteer, unautomated process.
  • Log virtual-experience lessons in the retro.

docs.title: Conference Chair
docs.text: The Conference Chair leads the conference organizing effort and is held by the Foundation President. The Chair runs the planning cycle, keeps the five committee leads unblocked, and owns the record of the year.

docs.title: Pre-Event
docs.text:
• Run the kickoff meeting at Month -8 (mid-August): assign committee leads via round-robin volunteer mapping, set the year's goals (sell-out date, profit target, meeting discipline), and set the CFP open date (October 1) as the cycle's first hard deadline.
  • Stand up the year's Important Documents at kickoff: minutes doc, Drive folder, budget sheet, and retro doc. The retro doc exists from day one and accumulates all year.
  • Host recurring planning meetings with a 45-minute target and a hard 1-hour cutoff. Committees report in fixed order (Chair, Speaker, Finance, Marketing, Venue, Community), each lead gives a 5-minute update, and every action item gets an owner.
  • Split large topics (opportunity grant review, catering) into special sessions instead of stretching the regular meeting.
  • Keep a standing Upcoming Deadlines block in the minutes with hard payment dates; rolling-template minutes lose action items without it, and small tasks stay "next week's problem" for weeks.
  • Run next-year planning inside the current cycle: sign next year's venue contract right after the conference, conflict-check dates about 11 weeks out against the Austin events spreadsheet, pay the deposit about 9 weeks out, and start theme and logo work. See ../runbooks/next-year-planning.md.
  • Own the run of show: keep a pitch-slot draft before sponsorships are sold so pitch slots can be written into contracts, and build the final grid about 2 weeks out. The grid tends to slip to the last few days; hold the two-week target. See ../runbooks/run-of-show.md.
  • Act as the escalation point when a committee is blocked or a vendor goes quiet.
  • Onboard any new committee lead against the prior year's folders and the last two retros. See ../runbooks/onboarding-new-lead.md.

docs.title: Day of Event
docs.text:
• Arrive at venue open (6:00 AM) and act as day-of lead.
  • Emcee opening and closing remarks, announcements, and door prize drawings; delegate as desired.
  • Work the run of show and unblock whoever is stuck. Standing retro advice: do not panic at the conference chair until at least day two.

docs.title: Post Event
docs.text:
• Launch the post-event survey on the last day of the conference.
  • Hold the retro meeting within two weeks; the retro doc has been filling all year.
  • Close out the conference year: confirm next year's contract and dates are locked, archive the Drive folder, and hand working docs to the next cycle's leads.

docs.title: Finance Chair
docs.text: The Finance Chair leads the Finance Committee: the budget, sponsorship end to end, registration money, grants, insurance, and taxes.

docs.title: Pre-Event
docs.text:
• Steward the budget sheet: a single guarded spreadsheet owned by the finance lead ("look, don't edit"), with target vs actual per line. Create next year's sheet during the current conference weekend.
  • Run sponsorship end to end: finalize the prospectus for publication by early October to hit corporate budget season, email it to the sponsor mailing list, clone per-tier contract templates, invoice (net 30, benefits secured only on full payment), and chase payment. See ../runbooks/sponsorship.md.
  • Sequence dependent orders behind sponsor payment; the lanyard order waits for the lanyard sponsor.
  • Know prospects' fiscal-year ends; deals close when a prospect's budget is about to expire, so time the ask to their calendar.
  • File the weekly Pretix accounting report every Monday from about 14 weeks out through conference week.
  • Open the opportunity grant application about 4 months out, close it around Week -8.5, and review applications in a dedicated special meeting the next day. Comp local ticket-only requests instead of spending grant funds, prioritize accepted speakers, and publish a per-person guidance range. See ../runbooks/grants.md.
  • Apply for the PSF grant about 3 months out; it requires a published schedule, CoC and policy links, and a budget, and carries an 8-week processing lead. External freezes happen without warning, so earlier is safer.
  • Buy event insurance through The Event Helper by Week -4.5. This is a hard deadline; keep it headlining the Upcoming Deadlines block so it cannot slip.
  • Remind vendors that 501(c)(3) status removes sales tax on orders.
  • Manage both bank accounts (Grasshopper Bank plus the credit union account) and report balances at planning meetings.
  • Publish the Sponsor KBYG about 5 weeks out and maintain the sponsor marketing sheet with its "Approved To Market?" gate; unpaid sponsors never get a post.

docs.title: Day of Event
docs.text:
• Chase final sponsor payments; this reliably runs into conference week.
  • Confirm sponsors receive their contracted benefits (booth table, pitch slot, shoutouts) and that comped sponsor tickets are actually redeemed; unredeemed comps go unnoticed without a check.
  • Handle day-of paid swag through Pretix voucher QR codes, not cash.

docs.title: Post Event
docs.text:
• Pay final vendor installments (the A/V final installment lands a few weeks after the conference).
  • Track opportunity grant fulfillment to completion (email sent, funds sent, ticket sent).
  • Produce the final accounting: revenue, expenses, and profit against the year's goal.
  • Wrap remaining reimbursements and file taxes.

docs.title: Marketing Chair
docs.text: The Marketing Chair leads the Marketing Committee: social campaigns, the newsletter, the website, and the design asset library. The mailing list is the workhorse channel and drives most ticket sales.

docs.title: Pre-Event
docs.text:
• Start social promotion 3-6 months out at minimum; paid ads are not used.
  • Get the year's website repo live before October 1 so the monthly newsletter on the 1st can link it.
  • Run the milestone campaigns: CFP announcement (October 1), prospectus publicity, early bird launch and countdown, speaker "Guess Who" teaser and reveal series (two posts per speaker across five platforms, starting mid-January), grant deadline, shirt last-chance, and sponsor thank-yous.
  • Send the Mailchimp newsletter monthly, then weekly near the event.
  • Keep the weekly cadence themes running between milestones: Monday quotes, Wednesday tutorial recordings, Friday community content.
  • Build the reusable Canva campaign brand template early in the cycle, not in the final month. Produce assets in three sizes per campaign.
  • Schedule posts through Buffer across LinkedIn, X, Bluesky, Fosstodon/Mastodon, and Facebook. Mastodon requires 720px minimum GIFs; design assets accordingly.
  • List the CFP on python.org events and pythondeadlin.es; offer CFP-writing help via Discord.
  • Enforce the "Approved To Market?" gate: sponsors get zero promotion until Finance confirms payment.
  • Run daily sponsor countdown posts across the final two weeks; the contractual obligation is one shoutout, practice is one before and one during.
  • Announce on Meetup.com to the Texas Python meetups and do a website freshness pass (Speak section, sponsor page, what-to-bring page) about 3 weeks out.
  • Skip mass-emailing universities; it produces nothing. Go for CS-club-level personal engagement instead.
  • Prepare the feedback form and organizer-interest form before the conference.

docs.title: Day of Event
docs.text:
• Post the sponsor thank-you and live-event content as scheduled.
  • Capture photos and short clips for post-event use.

docs.title: Post Event
docs.text:
• Promote the post-event survey; responses run about 2 weeks.
  • Export Buffer analytics and file photos.
  • Publish the recordings: the vendor delivers unlisted YouTube videos, and each video and the playlist must be flipped public.
  • Run the replay drip: one recorded talk promoted per week, every Wednesday, starting about 13 weeks after the conference and running about 16 weeks, across five platforms, with a GIF per talk. Sponsored talks are included.

docs.title: Speaker Chair
docs.text: The Speaker Chair leads the Speaker Committee: the CFP, talk selection, keynotes, tutorials, the schedule, and all speaker communications.

docs.title: Pre-Event
docs.text:
• Open the keynote nomination form (Google Form) at kickoff and close it end of September.
  • Run the keynote organizer election in early October: ranked ballot, +2 to -2 scoring, then a decided invite order. Work down the list and keep the backup order intact; invitations often go several names deep before someone accepts.
  • Open the CFP on Pretalx October 1, the cycle's first hard deadline, and close it early December.
  • Ask in the CFP whether selected speakers will need travel assistance; the answers feed opportunity grant planning.
  • Recruit tutorial presenters by direct invitation, starting with PyCon hallway conversations about 11 months out. Tutorials are not part of the open CFP.
  • Run talk review over the holidays, at least 2 full weeks: voting in Pretalx, then an in-person decision meeting.
  • Notify speakers around the new year with a hard confirmation deadline of about 2 weeks. Hold an ordered waitlist with the top candidates flagged, reject everything below the waitlist promptly, and offer standby speakers free tickets.
  • Send the speaker information form at acceptance and collect name, socials, and photo then; most speakers do not respond to later requests, and marketing stalls waiting on them.
  • Publish the schedule with slack for late dropouts; expect at least one within the final few weeks. Present the schedule to the planning meeting about 7.5 weeks out.
  • Get Slido and StageTimer single-event quotes about 7.5 weeks out.
  • Treat remote talks as high-risk and rehearse the audio path end to end; a remote talk with broken audio is the program failure attendees remember most.
  • Send the speaker KBYG about 2 weeks out, open the slide-upload folder, and collect technical-term lists for caption prep.
  • Build per-day lightning talk signup forms in the final week.

docs.title: Day of Event
docs.text:
• Brief speakers in person at the Friday appreciation dinner; speakers do not read email.
  • Run speaker tech checks Friday before 9:00 or at lunch; catch-as-catch-can between stage events on the weekend.
  • Keep the program on time with StageTimer and run Q&A through Slido. Never let the schedule run early; have filler trivia ready.
  • Seat the on-deck speaker when the prior talk begins; each 30-minute block is a 25-minute talk plus 5 minutes of Q&A and changeover.
  • Curate lightning talks: 8-9 slots per day, and submissions exceed slots.

docs.title: Post Event
docs.text:
• Distribute per-speaker feedback compiled from Slido and the feedback form.
  • Feed speaker-experience lessons into the retro.

docs.title: Venue Chair
docs.text: The Venue Chair leads the Venue Committee: the venue relationship, A/V, catering, evening events, alcohol compliance, swag, badges, signage, the registration desk, and volunteers.

docs.title: Pre-Event
docs.text:
• Manage the venue relationship (Austin Central Public Library, Special Event Center) and contract logistics. Access is 6:00 AM to 7:00 PM Friday through Sunday; there is no Thursday access, so setup happens Friday morning in parallel with tutorials.
  • Start A/V vendor outreach about Month -7, request the quote about Month -5.5, and expect the deposit about 3 months out. See ../runbooks/av.md.
  • Set the ticket timeline and stand up Pretix with demographic questions: early bird opens December 1 and closes mid-January. See ../runbooks/registration.md.
  • Run catering: ideation docs with headcount assumptions about 11 weeks out, quotes 8-10 weeks out, deposits (roughly half of totals) about 6.5 weeks out, final orders about 4.5 weeks out. Build the catering plan sheet with per-day blocks and a "who's getting what" shopping tab with an owner per item. See ../runbooks/catering.md.
  • Plan the evening events: the Friday invite-only appreciation dinner (speakers, sponsors, organizers, Friends of PyTexas, about 50-75) and the Saturday network event (about 150). See ../runbooks/network-event.md.
  • Own alcohol compliance: TABC permit plus a hired licensed peace officer (two budgeted). Start months early; the officer hire can take a month of bounced emails, and TABC approval is slow enough that a permit submitted a few weeks out may still be in review the day before the event.
  • Run swag ordering: quotes about 8 weeks out, first order (patches, stickers, pins) about 6.5 weeks out, shirts ordered immediately after pre-orders close about 5 weeks out, everything ordered and approved by 2.5 weeks out. Do not let the print vendor alter the logo. See ../runbooks/swag.md.
  • Order badges through ConferenceBadges.com earlier than feels necessary; the order tends to slip into the final two weeks.
  • Order linens from American Party Rental (reuse last year's invoice); the library provides furniture but no linens.
  • Print signage the final week: about 6 standing signs and 5-10 single-page signs, mapped on the Miro board with Community. Check whether the library has sign holders.
  • Collect dietary restrictions well before the final week; gathering them in the last days leaves no time to adjust orders.
  • Recruit volunteers and build the day-of staffing plan, including registration desk shifts and shirt-table coverage. See ../runbooks/volunteers.md.
  • Pursue a hotel room block early and give it an owner; it gets raised repeatedly and stalls without one.

docs.title: Day of Event
docs.text:
• Run the registration desk: three-station flow (intake form scan, badge pickup, shirt pickup by poker chip), 2 on check-in laptops, 1-2 on badges, everything set by 8:00 exactly. Keep blank badges and a label printer for late registrants.
  • Run food service around the run of show: coffee pickup, delivery windows, setup and teardown at breaks, and supply runs (Costco and HEB) as the restock mechanism.
  • Keep the shirt table staffed and the distribution system working; stand up a waitlist form if sizes run short.
  • Photograph venue property at load-in and load-out to avoid disputes; ask the library for reserved organizer parking.
  • Apply the leftover-food policy decided in advance: give leftovers to library staff.

docs.title: Post Event
docs.text:
• Return rentals and reconcile vendor invoices with Finance.
  • Count leftovers to calibrate next year's orders (diet sodas, sparkling water, and fruit are the hits; muffins and kolaches get over-ordered).
  • Thank the venue staff and log venue lessons in the retro.

  • Confidence monitors for speakers
  • Sound system, speakers
  • Mics (handheld for Q&A, lapel for speakers)
  • Recording
  • Livestream (YouTube)
  • Captioning
  • Speaker timer display (Stagetimer)
  • Laptop connectivity (USB-C preferred, HDMI, dongles)

docs.title: Tutorial Space
docs.text:
• Projector
  • Sound + instructor mic
  • Power strips at every table (missing power is a recurring retro complaint)

docs.title: Common Areas
docs.text:
• PA for announcements
  • Schedule + sponsor display screens

docs.title: Rooftop Events (If Used)
docs.text:
• Audio system (wireless, outdoor-capable)
  • Lighting if evening
  • Weather contingency

docs.title: Vendor Selection
docs.text:
• Get quotes with a detailed equipment list
  • On-site tech support hours
  • Setup + breakdown included?
  • Recording + livestream + captioning services
  • Backup equipment availability
  • Payment terms + schedule
  • References from other conferences

Check references. Compare price vs capability vs support. A/V is one of the largest expense lines in the budget.

docs.title: Contract + Payment
docs.text: Payment follows the vendor's schedule; the usual pattern is a deposit at booking, an installment or two near the event, and a final installment a few weeks after. Sign with Conference Chair signoff. Coordinate payments with Finance; the due dates should headline the meeting deadlines block for months.

docs.title: Captioning
docs.text:
Captioning is expected by attendees; keep it in scope every year. It is funded by two Captioning-tier sponsors, whose logos appear on the all-day captions and on the permanent videos.

  • Confirm captioning in the vendor scope
  • Line up Captioning-tier sponsors with Finance
  • Collect speaker slides and technical-term text files ahead of time to feed caption prep (the speaker KBYG asks for these)
  • Decide the display method (stream overlay, on-stage screen)

Attendees have asked for a captions screen at tutorials too.

docs.title: Graphics + Overlays
docs.text:
• Review and approve overlay templates (lower thirds, intros, sponsor logos)
  • Provide PNG with transparency for stream backgrounds without being asked
  • Test with actual content
  • Approve before production
  • Send the A/V recap deck data to the vendor early

docs.title: Dongle + Cable Kit
docs.text:
Buy and stage: - Dell laptop dongles (HDMI, USB-C) - Apple laptop dongles (USB-C, Mini DisplayPort) - HP laptop dongles - HDMI cables (extra long for stage) - Extension cords - Power strips - Gaffer tape

Projector issues are the #1 A/V problem. Have backups for every common laptop.

See day-of-supplies.md.

docs.title: Speaker Timer and Q&A Software
docs.text:
Stagetimer (stagetimer.io) and Slido are both bought as single-event licenses; get quotes for both around Week -7.5 (one Stagetimer login is enough). The single-event Stagetimer license is worth the cost.

  • Timer visible to speaker (confidence monitor or floor display)
  • Time warnings: 5 min, 2 min, wrap
  • Phone or tablet backup running Stagetimer if the main display fails
  • Slido handles Q&A and moderation and feeds per-speaker feedback after the event

docs.title: Tech Checks
docs.text: Windows: Friday before 9:00 AM or at lunch; catch-as-catch-can between stage events on the weekend. Speakers do not read email; brief them in person at the Friday evening event and walk them through the check-in flow. Remote talks are high-risk: an audio failure on a remote talk draws more criticism than any other program problem. Schedule a dedicated rehearsal for any remote speaker.

docs.title: Week Before
docs.text:
• Test all equipment in venue if possible
  • Test recording + livestream end-to-end (test stream at least one week ahead; see the Community runbook)
  • Verify captioning workflow
  • Confirm speaker timer setup
  • Verify dongles work with sample laptops

docs.title: Friday Morning (Setup Day)
docs.text:
• Vendor on site for setup + testing (venue access from 6:00 AM; no Thursday access)
  • Test mics, monitors, livestream
  • Walk through the speaker check-in flow with the vendor
  • On-deck table setup with signage

docs.title: Morning (Each Day)
docs.text:
• Vendor arrives 2 hours before doors
  • Test A/V, mics, monitors, livestream, speaker timer
  • Mic check (vendors sometimes skip it; remind them)
  • Backup dongles staged at on-deck table

docs.title: Throughout
docs.text:
• Tech check during prior talk's Q&A (on-deck table)
  • Monitor livestream quality (rotate organizers; never one person all weekend)
  • Watch for audio issues
  • Manage speaker timer
  • Reset Slido per session

docs.title: Issues
docs.text:
• Projector won't display: try Dell/Apple/HP dongles; fall back to the speaker's laptop screen
  • Mic down: hot swap, batteries, vendor
  • Stream drops: known library bandwidth issue; hotspot failover has been judged impractical, so raise mitigation options with the A/V vendor ahead of time
  • Timer dies: phone backup running Stagetimer

docs.title: Recording
docs.text:
• Confirm recording consent per speaker (KBYG + acceptance email)
  • Vendor captures every session
  • Backup recording (separate device) if budget allows
  • Get raw files post-conference (cloud or drive handoff)

docs.title: Week 1
docs.text:
• Receive all raw recordings
  • Quality check (audio, video, captioning)
  • Final A/V installment with Finance (typically due a few weeks after)
  • Coordinate edits with Community

docs.title: Editing + Publishing
docs.text:
• Edit dead air, fix audio issues
  • Per-talk titles + descriptions
  • Speaker preview before public posting
  • Upload to YouTube, build playlist
  • Slide links per talk
  • Share links with speakers
  • Social announcement (recordings feed the replay drip campaign; see the Marketing runbook)

docs.title: YouTube Channel Publishing
docs.text:
The A/V vendor delivers videos as unlisted. Flipping the playlist to public is not enough. Each individual video also has to be flipped to public. Check both.

  • Send to team to proof watch (audio, video, subtitles all line up and are correct)
  • Set playlist to public
  • Set all videos to public

Channel homepage: - [ ] Add the new year's playlist as a featured section - [ ] Reorder so the most recent year sits at the top - [ ] Past years stack below in reverse-chronological order

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
• Vendor performance: quality, support, responsiveness, value
  • Document for next year
  • Would use again?

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Projector issues are #1. Test early. Have dongles for Dell, Apple, HP.
  • Audio quality is a persistent retro complaint: dead time between talks, mic clarity, hallway echo bleeding into the room, stream cutouts and blur. Mic checks at the top of every day.
  • Power outlets at tables draw complaints every year. Bring power strips, especially for tutorials.
  • No proven mitigation for library bandwidth dips is on record; work options with the A/V vendor before the event.

docs.title: Budget Planning Template
docs.text: Structure for the year's budget sheet, based on the instrument PyTexas actually runs. One Google Sheet per year, created during the prior conference weekend, owned by the finance lead. Anyone can look; nobody edits without talking to the owner. Live numbers stay in the guarded sheet in the year's Drive folder; this page carries structure and percent-of-budget ranges only.

docs.title: Sheet Layout
docs.text:
Revenue block and Expenses block sit side by side on one tab.

Each revenue line tracks: Qty Sold, Price/Unit, Actual Revenue, Qty Available, Target Revenue. Each expense line tracks: Budget, Qty, Price/Unit, Cost, vs Budget, Notes. The Notes column doubles as a payment log: record when deposits went out and when money moved between lines (redirected honoraria, grant-fund transfers). Speakers redirect or donate honoraria into the opportunity grant fund most years; the Notes column is where that trail lives.

docs.title: Sponsors
docs.text:
• One line per closed sponsor and one line per open tier (Platinum, Gold, Silver, Bronze/Community, Captioning, Lanyard, Food, Coffee, Network Event), each with a target count.
  • Treat the PSF grant as sponsorship revenue.

docs.title: Attendees
docs.text:
• Individual and corporate, each split early bird / regular
  • Corporate sponsor-discount and bulk-discount lines
  • Student
  • Zero-price comp classes: speakers, sponsors, orgs, under 18, freebies
  • Discount-code tiers
  • Virtual, free and paid

docs.title: Misc
docs.text:
• Shirts, paid and free
  • Tutorial tickets: paid, student, free
  • Donations at three levels
  • Network Event tickets: paid, org, free

docs.title: Expense Categories
docs.text:
Eight categories, each with its own subtotal:

  1. Venue: rental, next-year deposit placeholder, insurance, peace officers (two), parking, signage. Rental is usually the largest single line.
  2. Food and Beverage: per-day breakfasts, per-day coffee service, snacks, tip, linens and misc. Usually the largest category overall; coffee is the recurring overrun, so budget it honestly.
  3. Happy Hour / Network Event: venue or buyout fee, food service, service charge and tip, vendor fees.
  4. A/V: sound and projection (large line), captioning, wifi, misc.
  5. Swag: lanyards, shirts, speaker gifts, badges, door prizes, stickers, misc, with design sub-lines.
  6. Speakers: keynote and tutorial honoraria, appreciation dinner venue and food, travel. The appreciation dinner food line tends to run over; budget it generously.
  7. Web: Pretix, Pretalx, Slido, StageTimer, Mailchimp, Buffer.
  8. Fees: Stripe processing, Pretix percentage, taxes.

docs.title: Percent-of-Budget Ranges
docs.text:
These shares are a planning heuristic, not derived from recorded actuals; treat them as starting points only.

Area Share of budget A/V 20-25% Network event 15-18% Venue 12-15% Catering 8-12% Swag 8-10% Opportunity grants 3-5% Reserve / contingency 10-15%

Speakers, web tooling, and payment fees take the small remainder.

In practice the relative magnitudes differ from the table: food and beverage is usually the largest expense category, happy hour / network event second, and venue rental the largest single line. Where the table and recorded actuals disagree, trust the actuals.

docs.title: Dashboard Metrics
docs.text:
Summary rows at the bottom of the sheet:

  • Percent of revenue goal
  • Percent of capacity
  • Percent of in-person capacity
  • Budgeted expense vs planned max revenue
  • Budgeted expense vs actual revenue
  • Current spend vs actual revenue (the post-event bottom line)

docs.title: Break-Even and Scenario Model
docs.text:
Keep a scenarios tab alongside the main sheet:

  • Break-even attendance at each realistic sponsorship level
  • What happens if a tier goes unsold, or if ticket sales land at half of capacity
  • The catering plan's maximum spend cap feeds in from catering.md

The sell-out number is 250 in-person, stretchable to 275; model against those, not aspirational counts.

docs.title: Tracking Cadence
docs.text:
• Update actuals weekly once ticket sales open (the weekly Pretix accounting report feeds this)
  • Read the bottom line at each planning meeting
  • Log every deposit and payment date in the Notes column
  • Flag variances to the Conference Chair early

Red flags:

  • Ticket sales pacing behind goal; a third of capacity sold at 5 weeks out means the sell-out goal is already gone
  • Sponsorship falling behind target with no pipeline to close the gap
  • Unbudgeted expense lines appearing

docs.title: Budget Calendar
docs.text:
• Month -12: create next year's sheet during the current conference weekend
  • Month -8: present at kickoff, settle targets
  • Month -6 to -3: lock A/V, venue balance, and vendor costs as contracts land
  • Weeks -8 to -2.5: swag and catering actuals land
  • Week -4.5: insurance purchased (hard deadline)
  • Week +3.5: final A/V installment
  • Post-event: reconcile actuals per line, document variances, hand tax records to the treasurer

docs.title: Catering Runbook
docs.text:
Venue Committee owns this. Covers breakfast, coffee, snacks, and all-day beverages for all three conference days. Lunch is never catered; see the Lunch section below. Evening events (Friday appreciation dinner, Saturday network event) are covered in network-event.md.

Food and beverage is the largest expense category in the budget, and the catering plan carries a hard maximum spend cap that feeds budget-planning-template.md.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
• Week -11: write the catering ideas doc: headcount assumptions, candidate vendors with menu links and minimums, a reminder to ask about nonprofit discounts
  • Weeks -10 to -8: gather quotes; remind vendors the 501(c)(3) status removes sales tax
  • Week -8.5: confirm headcounts and deposit amounts in a dedicated special session, not the regular meeting
  • Week -6.5: pay deposits (roughly half of each total)
  • Week -6: build the catering plan sheet (structure below)
  • Week -4.5: place final orders; order linens (American Party Rental; re-send last year's invoice)
  • Weeks -2 to -1: collect dietary restrictions; the final week is too late
  • Days -4 to -1: final plan updates; confirm delivery windows with every vendor
  • Friday morning: Costco + HEB supply run during the first tutorial

docs.title: Current Vendor Stack
docs.text:
• Breakfast: Tacodeli taco delivery Saturday and Sunday before doors, roughly 1.5 to 2 tacos per attendee per day, flour and corn, with vegetarian and vegan lines. Kolaches added Sunday.
  • Coffee: Doxa barista coffee bar Saturday and Sunday, heavily praised in attendee feedback and worth the cost; manage the line so people do not miss talk openings. Houndstooth urn pickup is the alternative: urns picked up before doors, returned after lunch. Central Market coffee boxes cover Friday.
  • Friday breakfast: Central Market muffins, fruit, and coffee boxes.
  • Afternoon break: Central Market platters (cookies, mini tartlets) delivered mid-afternoon.
  • Bulk snacks, sodas, and paper goods: Costco + HEB runs.
  • Ice: ordered online. This works well; repeated store runs are the fallback restock mechanism and eat organizer time.

Delivery windows go in the plan sheet: breakfast before doors open, the afternoon platters during the mid-afternoon break. Set the exact clock times with each vendor every year; they shift with that year's schedule. Get quotes carefully: some vendor sites show menu pricing, and catering pricing only appears once you start an order.

docs.title: The Catering Plan Sheet
docs.text:
One spreadsheet, built about Week -6 and updated through the day before the conference:

  1. One column block per day (Friday, Saturday, Sunday) plus a Costco misc block.
  2. Rows grouped by use: Breakfast, Breakfast Service/Delivery, Coffee, Snacks After Lunch, All-Day Beverages. Each row carries Item, Quantity, Cost Per, Total.
  3. Per-day estimated and actual totals, tax and tip lines, and an event-wide total against the stated maximum.
  4. A "Who's Getting What" second tab: item-level shopping quantities (sodas by flavor, sparkling water, bottled water, fruit by the pound, plates/napkins/cutlery counts) with an Organizer column naming who buys each item.

Tip on tips: set the tip percentage deliberately at order time; a mis-entered tip cannot be corrected after the order is placed.

docs.title: Dietary Handling
docs.text:
• Order vegetarian and vegan taco lines and label them at the table
  • Keep dedicated gluten-free and nut-free snack lines in the shopping tab
  • Label food with allergen information
  • Collect dietary restrictions from speakers and dinner guests earlier than the final week

docs.title: Lunch
docs.text:
Lunch is deliberately not catered on any day. Attendees get a long lunch break (roughly 12:30-2:00) and walk out in organizer-led groups to pre-picked nearby restaurants, each with an assigned captain. This doubles as a networking tactic.

  • Pick restaurants before conference week; keep an avoid list of venues that were slow in past years
  • Check Sunday opening hours for every restaurant on the list
  • Assign a captain per restaurant per day
  • Put the restaurant map on a slide shown before lunch dismissal

Lunch planning lands late every year; start it well before conference week.

docs.title: Quantity Calibration
docs.text:
Count leftovers every year and feed the counts back into next year's plan. Known calibration data:

  • Diet and zero sodas, sparkling water, and fruit are the hits; among regular sodas, Coke goes fastest and Dr Pepper gets left over.
  • Bananas go fast: budget about one per two to three attendees per day (a full-capacity weekend runs through 40-50 lb).
  • Muffins and kolaches tend to be over-ordered; order fewer.
  • Buy light on Friday to gauge the year's preferences, then buy in bulk for the weekend.
  • Any food put out is gone within an hour, except one unpredictable "forbidden item of the year."
  • Estimate quantities per person and extrapolate with a formula instead of guessing bulk numbers.

docs.title: Day-Of Mechanics
docs.text:
• Coffee pickup before doors (if using urn pickup); return urns after lunch
  • Breakfast delivery before doors; food set up before registration opens
  • Tear down food after breakfast and after the afternoon snack window; food out for an hour is food gone
  • Afternoon delivery arrives during the mid-afternoon break; have a table clear for it
  • Restock via store runs as needed; the shopping tab names who runs
  • Leftover policy, decided in advance: give leftovers to library staff
  • Count leftovers at teardown for next year's calibration

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Coffee is the largest catering friction and the recurring budget overrun; plan it first, not last.
  • Breakfast, coffee, and snack planning starts late every year; the timeline above is the fix.
  • Store runs eat organizer time; consider a full-service caterer or kitchen space.

docs.title: Call for Proposals Runbook
docs.text:
Speaker Committee owns this. Platform: Pretalx.

See speaker-committee-runbook.md for full speaker workflow.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
• October 1: CFP opens
  • December 1: early bird tickets open
  • Early December: CFP closes
  • December (holidays): review (min 2 full weeks)
  • Early January: speaker notifications
  • Mid-January: speaker list announced
  • Mid-January: early bird closes

Start CFP prep 2 months before opening.

docs.title: Pretalx Setup
docs.text:
• Create/update conference: https://pretalx.com/pytexas-[YEAR]
  • Configure submission form: title, abstract (public), description (reviewer), bio, headshot, socials, contact, level (Beg/Int/Adv), notes; talks are a single 30-minute length (25-minute talk plus 5 minutes of Q&A and changeover)
  • Include a travel-assistance question (will the speaker need help getting here?); answers feed opportunity grant planning, see grants.md
  • Set deadline
  • Configure reviewer accounts
  • Update email templates
  • Test submission end-to-end

docs.title: Marketing Coordination
docs.text:
• Announcement graphics + copy
  • Social campaign schedule
  • Newsletter announcement (1st of month)
  • Site updates
  • Discord post

docs.title: Past Speaker Outreach
docs.text:
Direct outreach to past speakers generates quality submissions; treat it as a core part of the campaign, not an extra.

  • Confirm access to the per-year past-speaker Google Group (a new group each year; check with the outgoing speaker chair)
  • Prepare CFP invitation email for past speakers

docs.title: Launch Day
docs.text:
• Open submissions in Pretalx
  • Send past-speaker invitations
  • Post: social (Buffer), newsletter, site, PyTexas Discord, Python community Slacks/Discords, LinkedIn/Mastodon/BlueSky/Twitter

docs.title: Reminders
docs.text:
• Mid-window push (~November 1), including the Texas meetup lists
  • Final week countdown before close

docs.title: Support
docs.text:
• Respond to inquiries within 24-48 hours
  • Optional office hours if submission volume low

docs.title: Phase 1: Individual Review (Weeks 1-2)
docs.text:
Reviewers in Pretalx: - Read all submissions - Score in Pretalx system - Notes on fit, experience level, topic, concerns

Scoring criteria: - Content quality (abstract clear? description shows depth?) - Audience fit (level + community relevance) - Clarity (can you tell what the talk covers?) - Timing (can they fit our time limits?)

docs.title: Phase 2: Committee Discussion (Week 3)
docs.text:
Format: in-person or video.

Agenda: 1. Top-scored (auto-accepts) 2. Middle tier (discussion) 3. Bottom tier (likely rejects) 4. Final accepted list 5. Waitlist 6. Track + schedule integration

Record the selection rationale; it is institutional memory for next year's committee.

docs.title: Acceptance (Early January)
docs.text: Email includes: - Conference dates + venue - Response deadline (1-2 weeks) - Confirm acceptance - Updated bio if needed - High-res headshot - Social handles - A/V requirements - Accessibility needs - Speaker benefits (free ticket, Friday appreciation dinner) - Speaker resources link

docs.title: Rejection
docs.text:
Send at notification time, alongside the acceptances: reject everything below the ordered waitlist promptly. Only waitlisted speakers wait; keep the waitlist ordered (roughly 10 deep) with the top few flagged.

Email: - Thanks for submitting - Encourage conference attendance - Invite resubmission next year - Optional feedback if requested

docs.title: Waitlist
docs.text:
• Keep the waitlist ordered, with the top candidates flagged
  • Don't reject waitlisted speakers initially; promote in order on declines
  • Offer standby speakers free tickets
  • Send waitlist rejections once all accepted speakers have confirmed

docs.title: Speaker Announcement (Mid-January)
docs.text:
• Update site with speaker lineup
  • Speaker spotlight graphics for social (the "Guess Who" teaser-then-reveal series)
  • Remind attendees early bird closes mid-January

docs.title: Speaker Info Collection
docs.text:
Send the speaker information form (Google Form) with the acceptance email, not later. Chasing this data after the fact is painful; response rates crater once the acceptance moment passes.

  • High-res headshot
  • Social handles
  • Pronouns
  • Company affiliation (if listed)
  • Short bio
  • Final talk title + public abstract

docs.title: Cross-Committee
docs.text:
• Marketing: promo + social
  • Venue: A/V requirements, accessibility
  • Venue: Friday appreciation dinner headcount
  • Community: Discord + virtual engagement

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text: Tutorials are recruited by direct invitation, not through the open CFP. Start recruiting in person at PyCon, about 11 months out, and keep a ranked shortlist with backups. Tutorial recruiting runs earlier than the talk CFP because tutorials need more prep.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
• Pretalx (conference page at pretalx.com/pytexas-[YEAR])
  • The past-speaker Google Group and CFP campaign docs live in the year's Drive folder

docs.title: Code of Conduct Runbook
docs.text:
The policy of record is the PyTexas Code of Conduct published on pytexas.org. This page covers operations: how reports come in, who responds, and how incidents are handled. It does not restate or replace the policy text.

Owned by Community Committee; the Conference Chair is the escalation point.

docs.title: Before the Conference
docs.text:
• Confirm the CoC is current and linked from the website, the ticket flow, and the Attendee KBYG
  • Identify the response team: multiple trained responders, not one person
  • Brief responders on the reporting flow, the enforcement ladder below, and documentation
  • Put responder phone numbers in the Org Info Sheet roster
  • Confirm sponsor contracts bind sponsor representatives to the CoC (the standard sponsor agreement does this, and the Foundation holds a reputational-risk termination clause)
  • Brief Discord moderators on CoC handling and escalation

docs.title: Reporting Channels Day-Of
docs.text:
Attendees can report through any of these:

  • Any organizer in a staff shirt (the year's organizer color), in person
  • A direct message to a Discord moderator or organizer
  • The contact channel published in the CoC itself

Whoever receives a report brings it to a response-team member immediately. Serious incidents go straight to the Conference Chair. The report-taker does not adjudicate on the spot; they document and hand off.

docs.title: Enforcement Ladder
docs.text:
Minor (mild inappropriate comment):

  1. Warn privately, explain the issue
  2. Document
  3. Monitor

Moderate (persistent or hostile behavior):

  1. Serious private conversation
  2. Mute or timeout in Discord if online
  3. Document thoroughly, inform the Conference Chair
  4. Ask the person to leave if in person and the behavior continues

Serious (harassment, discrimination, threats):

  1. Immediate removal from the venue or ban from the server
  2. Inform the Conference Chair immediately
  3. Venue security if needed; police if criminal
  4. Document everything
  5. Follow up with the person who was targeted
  6. Ban from future events

This ladder applies equally to attendees, speakers, volunteers, organizers, and sponsor representatives.

docs.title: Incident Documentation
docs.text:
Fill this out for every report, including ones resolved with a quiet word:

Date/time:
Location (channel or physical):
Reported by:
Reported to:
People involved:
Description:
CoC violation(s):
Action taken:
Follow-up needed:
Reported to Conference Chair: Y/N
Police contacted: Y/N
Notes:

Records go to the Conference Chair and are kept out of shared committee folders.

docs.title: After the Conference
docs.text:
• Confirm every incident record is complete and any follow-up done
  • Follow up with reporters on outcomes where appropriate
  • Bring a count and any process lessons (not identifying details) to the retro
  • Update this page and the response-team briefing with what was learned

docs.title: Cross-Committee
docs.text:
• Finance: CoC language in sponsor contracts
  • Speaker: CoC expectations in speaker comms and the speaker KBYG
  • Community: Discord moderation, day-of visibility
  • Conference Chair: escalation, records, final calls on removal or bans

docs.title: Community Committee Runbook
docs.text:
Responsibilities: community outreach to the four Texas metro meetups, attendee communications and aftercare, the virtual and hybrid experience, Discord server and bot, YouTube streaming operations, group walks and networking formats, and signage maps.

See discord.md, post-event.md, feedback.md, coc.md.

Attendance context for planning:

  • In-person sells out around 250, stretchable to ~275.
  • Virtual ticket sales are tiny regardless of the cap; expect a handful to a few dozen.

Treat virtual as a low-cost overflow channel, not a second audience to size for.

docs.title: Engagement Plan
docs.text:
• Review prior year: retro doc, survey results, what worked, attendance patterns
  • Review the virtual event format against last year's retro; decide what virtual attendees get this year
  • Plan meetup and online engagement leading up to the conference

docs.title: Discord
docs.text:
• Review server structure, roles, bot, moderation
  • Plan improvements (channels, bot features, onboarding, virtual experience)
  • Confirm the bot has a maintainer and at least one second maintainer

docs.title: Code of Conduct
docs.text:
• Confirm the CoC is current and posted; identify and brief the response team

See coc.md for reporting channels, responders, and the enforcement ladder.

docs.title: Month -7 to -5: Discord Setup and Communications
Discord Setup
docs.text:
• Archive old conference channels
  • Create new year channels: #general, #announcements, #cfp-discussions, #speakers, #sponsors, #virtual-attendees, #help, #random, #job-board, voice channels
  • Roles: Organizer, Speaker, Sponsor, Attendee (in-person), Attendee (virtual), Volunteer
  • Test bot: /register, role assignment, ticket verification, error handling
  • Update server icon and banner

/register fails on bulk corporate purchases because the registering email is the buyer's, not the attendee's. Have a manual role-assignment override ready. See discord.md.

docs.title: Bot Improvements
docs.text:
• Review prior-year issues
  • Scope slash commands to what will actually exist by conference time: /poll, /question, /schedule first
  • Run bot changes like software: PR review, demos at planning meetings
  • Document known workarounds

docs.title: Communications Plan
docs.text:
• Plan email touchpoints: CFP open, early bird, CFP close, schedule, regular tickets, pre-conference reminders, day-before, thank you, survey
  • Build templates (see below)
  • Coordinate with Finance (ticket emails) and Marketing
  • Ticket messaging must state which days each ticket covers; when the site lists a three-day range, attendees without tutorial tickets show up Friday

docs.title: Intake Form
docs.text:
• Push for integration into ticket purchase (not a separate form)
  • Questions: dietary, accessibility, shirt size, first-timer, source, opportunity grant, virtual/in-person, emergency contact
  • Capture speaker Discord handles at speaker intake (coordinate with Speaker Committee)
  • Emergency-contact data gets deleted after the conference; see feedback.md
  • Test end-to-end; confirm data is accessible to committees

docs.title: Community Outreach
docs.text:
• Ping the four Texas metro meetups: Austin, DFW, Houston, San Antonio
  • Meetup presentations, community announcements, cross-promotion
  • Free virtual tickets for meetup organizers as a thank-you

docs.title: Networking Formats
docs.text:
• Recruit walk leaders for organizer-led group lunches
  • Plan Open Spaces in a side area; schedule them opposite talks as little as possible
  • Plan a nature walk or similar lunch activity with a recruited leader
  • Post-event surveys keep asking for more networking formats (roundtables, breakout sessions, a women-of-Python gathering); consider adding one

docs.title: Day-of Coordination Tool
docs.text:
• Pick ONE chat tool for day-of coordination and commit to it
  • Juggling Discord plus Slack plus Slido simultaneously is painful; do not do it

docs.title: Streaming Coverage Plan
docs.text:
• Name the primary streaming and chat operator
  • Train at least one backup who knows the full YouTube plus Discord workflow
  • A solo operator all weekend is an illness away from no stream

docs.title: Slido
docs.text:
• Single-event license; moderation settings to block spam
  • Brief moderators (approve, filter, mark answered, archive per talk)
  • Test the workflow

docs.title: Final Weeks
docs.text:
• Test stream at least one week ahead
  • Send the "1 week before" email
  • Daily Discord countdown
  • Final bot test, coverage confirmed, critical info pinned
  • Virtual attendee welcome: stream access, Discord join, /register, Slido, schedule
  • Build the post-event survey and distribution email; see feedback.md
  • Print signage from the Miro sign map; check whether the library has sign holders (coordinate with Venue)

docs.title: Every Day
docs.text:
• Go live 10-15 minutes before the first session
  • Welcome post in #general with a CoC reminder
  • Start and maintain the link-compilation doc: every link shared in the conference-chat channel gets compiled into one doc, organized per day; the compiled doc becomes a lasting artifact
  • Monitor channels, respond to registration issues, manual role assignment for /register failures

docs.title: Per Talk
docs.text:
• Post speaker info as each talk starts: name, LinkedIn or handles, talk title, slides link when available; attendees appreciate these posts
  • Moderate Slido before display; archive questions after each talk
  • Point overflow Q&A to the conference-chat channel; speakers answer there after their slots

docs.title: In Person
docs.text:
• Be visible; direct, troubleshoot, facilitate intros
  • Watch for CoC issues; see coc.md for the response process

docs.title: Survey and Feedback
docs.text:
• Launch the post-event survey on the last conference day; ~2 week response window; ~50 responses is typical
  • Compile per-speaker feedback from Slido and the feedback form; distribute to speakers
  • Delete emergency-contact data

See feedback.md and post-event.md.

docs.title: Aftercare
docs.text:
• Thank-you email to attendees (highlights, photos, recordings timeline, next year preview)
  • Thank moderators and volunteers
  • Keep Discord active: highlights, recording links, slide links, the compiled links doc
  • Archive conference channels after 2-4 weeks; maintain general channels year-round

docs.title: Recordings
docs.text:
• Coordinate with Speaker Committee and Marketing on publishing
  • Recordings land on pyvideo.org via a manual pull request to the pyvideo/data repo; this is one volunteer's manual work, not automated
  • Post links in Discord as talks publish

docs.title: Meetups
docs.text:
• Coordinate with the Foundation on the four metro meetups
  • Announce the conference at meetups, recruit speakers

docs.title: Online Community
docs.text:
• Keep Discord active year-round
  • Coordinate social with Marketing
  • Welcome newcomers

Organizer coordination also runs in Discord, with a webhook feeding ticket purchases into a channel.

docs.title: Cross-Committee
docs.text:
• Conference Chair: attendee feedback, escalations, major comms
  • Marketing: messaging alignment, social posts, survey promotion, replay campaign
  • Speaker: speaker info for Discord posts, speaker comms, Q&A flow, per-speaker feedback
  • Finance: registration issues, ticket comms, opportunity grant announcements
  • Venue: attendee logistics questions, accessibility, signage printing, A/V and stream coordination

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Bundle virtual access with in-person tickets and keep the virtual workload proportional to its tiny audience.
  • A separate intake form costs registration time; integrate it into ticket purchase.

docs.title: Conference Committee Runbook
docs.text:
Chair: Conference Chair (the Foundation President is the Conference Chair).

Responsibilities: overall coordination, committee oversight, meeting management, next-year planning, risk, escalation.

See conference-master-timeline.md, kickoff-meeting.md, next-year-planning.md.

docs.title: Meeting Discipline
docs.text:
• 45-minute target, hard cutoff at one hour, per-section timers in the agenda
  • Fixed committee report order: Chair, Speaker, Finance, Marketing, Venue, Community
  • 5-minute update slot per committee, split into "discussion for this time" and "items for next meeting"
  • Action items captured with owners and due dates
  • One running minutes doc for the whole cycle, newest meeting on top, reusable template at the bottom

Cadence ramps with the calendar: roughly monthly after kickoff, biweekly from January, weekly from about 9 weeks out. Fixed report order, per-section timers, and special sessions keep a small organizing team on one page inside an hour.

docs.title: Upcoming Deadlines Block
docs.text:
Keep a standing Upcoming Deadlines section in every agenda listing hard payment and order dates: insurance, catering deposits, shirt order close, TABC permit, badges, sponsor payments.

Rolling-template minutes lose action items without it. Small items stay "next week's problem" for weeks, and hard deadlines like insurance hold only when they headline this block.

docs.title: Special Sessions
docs.text: Split large decision work out of the regular meeting into dedicated special sessions so the regular meeting keeps its timers. Typical special sessions: opportunity grant review (the day after applications close) and catering deposits and headcounts.

docs.title: Next-Year Planning
docs.text: Next-year planning runs inside the current cycle, not after it. Dates are conflict-checked about 11 weeks before the current conference, the deposit goes down about 9 weeks out, and the venue contract is signed right after the current conference at the latest. See next-year-planning.md.

docs.title: Month -13 to -12: During and Just After the Previous Conference
docs.text:
• Sign next year's venue agreement and pay the deposit (see next-year-planning.md)
  • Create the new cycle's budget sheet and retro doc; the retro doc is live from day one
  • Launch the post-event survey on the last conference day (see post-event.md)
  • Hold the retro meeting within 2 weeks

docs.title: Month -12 to -9
docs.text:
• Refine the retro; carry action items into the new cycle
  • Review committee structure and identify gaps
  • Recruit organizers and candidate leads
  • Track logo work with Marketing (starts around Month -12 to -10)

docs.title: Month -8 (Mid-August): Kickoff
docs.text:
The kickoff is virtual, at Month -8 (mid-August). See kickoff-meeting.md for the full template.

  • Stand up the year's Important Documents: minutes doc, Drive folder, budget sheet, retro doc
  • Assign committee leads via round-robin volunteer mapping
  • Set annual goals: sell-out date, profit target, meeting discipline, process goals
  • Set the CFP open date (October 1) as the cycle's first hard deadline
  • Set up task tracking (Asana) and the chat platform
  • Set meeting cadence and clone the agenda template

Six units, each with a lead:

  1. Conference Chair (coordination, meetings, next-year planning, escalation)
  2. Speaker (CFP, talk selection, keynotes, tutorials, schedule, speaker comms)
  3. Finance (budget, sponsorship, registration money, grants, insurance, taxes)
  4. Marketing (social campaigns, newsletter, website, design assets)
  5. Venue (venue relationship, A/V, catering, evening events, swag, badges, registration desk, volunteers)
  6. Community (outreach, Discord, streaming, virtual experience, aftercare)

docs.title: Month -8 to -6
docs.text:
• Monitor CFP launch with Speaker (opens October 1)
  • Monitor prospectus publication with Finance (early October, to hit corporate budget season)
  • Monitor website launch with Marketing (live before October 1 for the newsletter)
  • Confirm A/V vendor outreach with Venue
  • Keep runbooks updated as decisions land; do not wait until after the conference

docs.title: Month -6 to -4
docs.text:
• Monitor early bird launch (December 1) with Finance and Venue
  • Monitor CFP close and talk review with Speaker (early December, review over the holidays)
  • Track ticket pacing against the sell-out goal; push marketing earlier if behind
  • Choose next year's dates and target a signed next-year contract by February 1 (see next-year-planning.md)

docs.title: Month -4 to -2
docs.text:
• Weekly status reviews across committees; resolve blockers immediately
  • Run the grant review special session (applications close ~Week -8.5)
  • Run the catering special session (deposits ~Week -8.5)
  • Budget watch with Finance
  • Keep the Upcoming Deadlines block current: insurance (Week -4.5), shirt pre-order close (~Week -5), TABC permit, badges
  • Confirm day-of roles and prevent organizer burnout

docs.title: Month -2 to Conference
docs.text:
• Weekly all-hands
  • Build the run of show final grid ~2 weeks out; a pitch-slot draft should have existed since before the prospectus shipped (see run-of-show.md)
  • Backup coverage for critical roles, including streaming
  • Brief volunteers
  • Confirm the phone-numbers roster in the Org Info Sheet; do not rely only on chat in emergencies
  • Emergency kit: gaffer tape, extension cords, markers, paper, first aid, chargers
  • Review final attendee emails with Community

docs.title: Conference Days
docs.text:
• Arrive at venue access (6:00 AM); the venue closes hard at 7:00 PM
  • Morning huddle with organizers
  • 8:55 set up opening remarks; deliver them at 9:00
  • Monitor operations and schedule adherence
  • Handle escalations and executive decisions
  • Check in with each committee during the day
  • End-of-day debrief, brief the team on the next day, thank the team

Delegation is the goal. The chair should not be the only one handling everything. "Don't panic at the conference chair until at least day two."

docs.title: Post-Conference
docs.text:
• Survey live from the last conference day (see post-event.md)
  • Public thanks: committees, sponsors, speakers, attendees
  • Retro meeting within 2 weeks; the retro doc has been accumulating all year
  • Update runbooks with lessons
  • Confirm the next cycle's Important Documents exist (they should, per next-year-planning.md)
  • Hand off to next year's chair if changing

docs.title: Escalation Paths
docs.text:
• Any issue: the relevant committee lead first, then the Conference Chair as the escalation point
  • Medical: 911, then notify the Conference Chair

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• The run of show grid slips to 3-4 days out unless it is scheduled; build it 2 weeks out, with a pitch-slot draft in hand before sponsorships are sold.
  • Ticket sales lag the sell-out goal unless marketing pushes start early and hit hard; track pacing from the first sale.
  • The conference chair is a single point of failure. Delegate harder than feels comfortable.
  • Volunteers need defined roles, not "whoever's free."
  • Document during the cycle, not after. Runbooks written after the conference lose the detail.

docs.title: Conference Master Timeline

For detail on any item, see the topic and committee runbooks.

docs.title: Month -13 to -12: During and Just After the Previous Conference
docs.text:
• [Chair] Sign next year's facility use agreement immediately after the current conference and pay the 50% deposit at signing (14-day return deadline). See next-year-planning.md.
  • [Finance] Create next year's budget sheet during the current conference weekend.
  • [Chair] Start the retro doc within days of the event; it accumulates all year.
  • [Marketing] Announce next year's dates at the current conference with a draft page; do not build the full site during the event itself.

docs.title: Month -12 to -9: Handoff and Branding
docs.text:
• [Marketing] Start logo work (~10 months out; aim to have it done before kickoff). The logo blocks the website, prospectus, and swag.
  • [Speaker] Recruit tutorial presenters in person, starting at PyCon US (~11 months out). Tutorials are invited directly, not part of the open CFP.
  • [Chair] Refine the retro; carry action items into the new cycle.

docs.title: Month -8: Kickoff
docs.text:
Kickoff is mid-August, about 8 months out. This is settled practice.

  • [Chair] Hold the kickoff meeting: virtual, 45-minute target, hard 1-hour cutoff. See kickoff-meeting.md.
  • [Chair] Assign committee leads via round-robin volunteer mapping; set annual goals (sell-out date, profit target, meeting discipline).
  • [Chair] Stand up the year's Important Documents: minutes doc, Drive folder, budget sheet, retro doc.
  • [Speaker] Open the keynote nomination form. See keynote.md.
  • [Speaker] Set the CFP open date (October 1) as the cycle's first hard deadline.

docs.title: Month -7: September
docs.text:
• [Marketing] Build the year's marketing planning docs and campaign templates; onboard any new lead against last year's folders and the last two retros. See onboarding-new-lead.md.
  • [Marketing] Get the year's website live before October 1 so the newsletter on the 1st can link it.
  • [Venue] Start A/V vendor outreach. See av.md.
  • [Finance] Finalize the sponsor prospectus for publication by early October, explicitly to hit corporate budget season. See sponsorship.md.
  • [Chair] Draft the run of show skeleton with pitch slots before any sponsorship is sold, so pitch slots can be written into contracts. See run-of-show.md.
  • [Speaker] Close keynote nominations end of September or early October.

docs.title: Month -6.5: October 1
docs.text:
• [Speaker] CFP opens October 1 on Pretalx; it runs to early December. See cfp.md.
  • [Finance] Publish the sponsor prospectus and email it to the sponsor mailing list.
  • [Marketing] Run the CFP announcement campaign: one Mailchimp email, same-day posts across platforms, Canva assets in three sizes, CFP-writing help via Discord, listings on pythondeadlin.es and python.org events.
  • [Speaker] Run the keynote organizer election (ranked ballot, +2 to -2 scoring).

docs.title: Month -5.5 to -5: Late October and November
docs.text:
• [Speaker] Decide the keynote invite order from the ranked list and work down it. Keep the full ranked list; invitations often go several names deep before someone accepts.
  • [Finance] Clone per-tier sponsor agreement templates from last year.
  • [Venue] Set the ticket timeline: early bird opens December 1, speaker list mid-January, early bird closes mid-to-late January. Start Pretix setup with demographic questions.
  • [Venue] Request the A/V quote and book the vendor.
  • [Venue] Amend the venue agreement if needed.
  • [Marketing] Push a CFP reminder to Texas meetup lists mid-window.

docs.title: Month -4.5: December 1
docs.text:
• [Venue] Early bird tickets open December 1 on Pretix, with caps by class and shirts sold as a pre-order add-on. See registration.md.
  • [Speaker] CFP closes early December. Review over the holidays for at least two full weeks: voting in Pretalx, then an in-person decision meeting.
  • [Finance] Open the opportunity grant application. See grants.md.
  • [Speaker] Send the speaker information form to accepted speakers in mid-December, not a week before the event.
  • [Finance] Have the sponsor invoice template ready.

docs.title: Month -3.5: Around January 1
docs.text:
• [Speaker] Send speaker notifications around the new year with a hard confirmation deadline (~2 weeks). Reject everything below the waitlist promptly; offer standbys free tickets.
  • [Finance] Apply for the PSF grant about 3 months out. It requires a published schedule, CoC and policy links, and a budget, and carries an 8-week processing lead. External freezes happen without warning, so earlier is safer.

docs.title: Week -14 to -12: Mid-to-Late January
docs.text:
• [Speaker] Confirm the talk lineup and hold an ordered waitlist.
  • [Finance] Pay the library invoice and the A/V deposit.
  • [Finance] Start weekly Pretix accounting reports, filed every Monday until conference week.
  • [Marketing] Speaker reveal January 15, with a teaser-then-reveal post pair per speaker across five platforms. Collect name, socials, and photo at acceptance, not later.
  • [Venue] Early bird ends around January 19; run a countdown campaign the week before.
  • [Chair] Choose next year's dates by conflict-checking the Austin events spreadsheet; target a signed next-year venue contract by February 1. See next-year-planning.md.
  • [Marketing] Issue Friends of PyTexas coupon codes via Pretix.

docs.title: Week -11 to -9: Late January and Early February
docs.text:
• [Chair] Pay next year's venue deposit.
  • [Speaker] Publish the schedule; confirm the tutorials.
  • [Venue] Open the swag ideation docs (shirt ideas, other swag, speaker gifts) and the catering ideas doc with headcount assumptions. See swag.md and catering.md.
  • [Venue] Gather catering, bartending, and swag quotes. Remind vendors that 501(c)(3) status removes sales tax.

docs.title: Week -8.5: Mid-February
docs.text:
• [Finance] Opportunity grant applications close around Week -8.5. Review them in a dedicated special meeting the next day, not the regular meeting.
  • [Venue] Confirm catering deposits and headcounts; deposits run roughly half of totals.

docs.title: Week -7.5 to -6: Late February and Early March
docs.text:
• [Speaker] Present the proposed schedule; get Slido and StageTimer single-event quotes.
  • [Venue] Pay the first swag order (patches, stickers, pins); pay both dinner-venue deposits.
  • [Venue] Build the catering plan sheet: per-day blocks (breakfast, coffee, snacks, all-day beverages) plus a "who's getting what" shopping tab with an owner per item.
  • [Venue] Submit the TABC permit for any alcohol service, and start the peace officer hire if not already running. Permit review is slow; a filing left to the final weeks can still be in review the day before the event, so file it here. See network-event.md.
  • [Finance] Chase remaining sponsor contracts; hold dependent orders behind sponsor payment (the lanyard order waits for the lanyard sponsor).

docs.title: Week -5.5 to -4.5: Mid-March
docs.text:
• [Finance] Buy event insurance by Week -4.5 (The Event Helper). Hard deadline.
  • [Venue] Close shirt pre-orders around Week -5 with a last-chance campaign, then place the shirt order immediately after, around Week -4.5.
  • [Venue] Confirm the licensed peace officer for alcohol service; hiring can take a month of bounced emails, so this should already be in motion.
  • [Venue] Place final catering orders; order linens (American Party Rental; reuse last year's invoice).
  • [Finance/Marketing] Publish the Attendee KBYG and Sponsor KBYG; build the sponsor marketing sheet with an "Approved To Market?" gate. Unpaid sponsors never get a post.
  • [Marketing] Prep sponsor thank-you campaigns per sponsor: one before, one during.

docs.title: Week -3.5 to -2.5: Late March
docs.text:
• [Marketing] Announce to Texas Python meetups on Meetup.com; run a website freshness pass (Speak section, sponsor page, what-to-bring page).
  • [Venue] Have all swag ordered and approved.
  • [Venue] Confirm the TABC permit is approved and in hand.
  • [Venue] Finalize both dinner plans.

docs.title: Week -1.5 to -1: Final Two Weeks
docs.text:
• [Speaker] Send the speaker KBYG; open the slide-upload folder; collect technical-term lists for caption prep.
  • [Community] Run a test stream at least one week ahead. See discord.md.
  • [Venue] Print signage (~6 standing signs, 5-10 single-page; map it on a Miro board); check whether the venue has sign holders.
  • [Venue] Order badges (ConferenceBadges.com). Badges tend to slip to the final two weeks; treat this as the latest acceptable moment, not the plan.
  • [Venue] Collect dietary restrictions now, not in the final week.
  • [Marketing] Run daily sponsor countdown posts; build the per-day lightning talk signup forms; prepare the feedback form and organizer-interest form.
  • [Finance] Chase final sponsor payments; this tends to run into conference week, so start early and keep dependent orders sequenced behind payment.

docs.title: Days -4 to -1: Conference Week
docs.text:
• [Chair] Finish the run of show grid. Left alone it gets built 3-4 days out; target ~2 weeks out instead. See run-of-show.md.
  • [Venue] Final catering plan updates; plan the Friday morning Costco and HEB run during the first tutorial.

docs.title: Conference Weekend
docs.text: There is no Thursday venue access. The contract covers three 13-hour days, Friday through Sunday, 6:00 AM to 7:00 PM. Setup happens Friday morning in parallel with tutorials. See day-of-operations-guide.md and run-of-show.md.

docs.title: Week +1 to +2: Post-Event
docs.text:
• [Community/Marketing] Launch the post-event survey on the last conference day; collect responses for about two weeks.
  • [Speaker] Distribute per-speaker feedback from Slido and the feedback form.
  • [Marketing] Export Buffer analytics; file photos.
  • [Chair] Hold the retro meeting within two weeks; the retro doc has been accumulating all year. See post-event.md.
  • [Finance] Pay the final A/V installment (typically due a few weeks after the conference).

docs.title: Month +3 Onward: Replays
docs.text:
• [Marketing] Run the replay drip: one recorded talk per week, every Wednesday, starting ~13 weeks after the conference and running ~16 weeks, across five platforms with a GIF per talk.
  • [Community] Get recordings onto pyvideo.org via a manual pull request to the pyvideo/data repo.
  • [Marketing] Flip each YouTube video and the playlist from unlisted to public; the vendor delivers them unlisted.

docs.title: Critical Path
docs.text:
Long lead time or blocks other work:

  1. Next-year venue contract: sign right after the current conference, deposit at signing.
  2. Logo (Months -12 to -10): blocks the website, prospectus, and swag.
  3. CFP opens October 1: the website must be live first.
  4. Prospectus by early October: corporate budget season does not wait.
  5. Run of show draft: a pitch-slot skeleton must exist before sponsorships are sold.
  6. A/V vendor: outreach Month -7, booked by Month -6 to -5, deposit by Month -3.
  7. Shirt pre-order close (~Week -5) and immediate order (~Week -4.5).
  8. Badges: a recurring late item; order before the final two weeks.

docs.title: Budget Ranges (% of Total)
docs.text:
These shares are a planning heuristic, not derived from recorded actuals; treat them as starting points only.

  • A/V: 20-25%
  • Networking event: 15-18%
  • Venue: 12-15%
  • Catering: 8-12%
  • Swag: 8-10%
  • Opportunity grants: 3-5%
  • Reserve: 10-15%

Actuals tend to differ: food and beverage runs largest, the network event second, and venue rental is the largest single line. Where the shares and your own records disagree, trust the records.

See budget-planning-template.md.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Ticket sales lag without active pushes. Start pushes earlier than feels necessary and track progress against the sell-out goal from early bird onward.
  • Coffee is the largest catering friction and a common budget overrun. Plan it deliberately.
  • Sponsors sometimes never redeem their comped tickets. Track redemption through the conference.
  • Library pricing may rise; get the next-year contract signed by February 1.
  • Order ice online. Repeated store runs are the fallback restock mechanism and eat organizer time.

docs.title: Day-of Operations Guide
docs.text:
Run-of-day for Friday setup plus tutorials and the Saturday/Sunday main conference. Pair with run-of-show.md for the minute-by-minute.

There is no Thursday venue access. The venue contract covers three 13-hour days, Friday through Sunday, 6:00 AM to 7:00 PM. All setup happens Friday morning, in parallel with tutorials.

docs.title: Friday: Setup and Tutorial Day
docs.text: Tutorials run 9:00-12:00 and 2:00-5:00, with a 90-minute sponsored workshop at 4:30. Registration is open 9:00-12:00 and 2:00-5:00. Friday is the light program day; use it to stage everything the weekend needs.

docs.title: Early Morning (6:00-9:00)
docs.text:
• 6:00 venue access; Conference Chair arrives at open
  • Coffee pickup before doors
  • Friday breakfast out (Central Market muffins, fruit, coffee boxes); buy light Friday to gauge preferences, then bulk-buy for the weekend
  • Registration, food, and linens setup before doors
  • Speaker tech checks for anyone on site before 9:00 (the other window is lunch)

Registration desk setup:

  • 3-table bubble layout, room for backpack drop
  • 2 laptops on check-in, power strip, label printer, backup lists, pens
  • Badges sorted alphabetically; blank badges staged for late registrants
  • Lanyards on stands, separate from badges
  • Numbered signs for the three-station flow: (1) intake form, (2) badge pickup, (3) shirt pickup by poker chip

Badge and shirt prep:

  • Bundle shirts with badges per buyer; bag shirts
  • Poker chips into badge bags for shirt buyers
  • Ribbons (meetup organizer, hiring, etc.) into bags if used
  • Shirt table sorted by size with size signs; keep it staffed

Tutorial room:

  • Power strips at every table (a perennial complaint when missed)
  • Test outlets, mics, projector, timer
  • Water out for instructors

Catering:

  • Coffee station, allergen signs, plates and napkins
  • Trash cans in multiple spots
  • See catering.md for the plan sheet and delivery windows

Signage:

  • Standing signs and single-page signs placed per the Miro board map
  • "Badge required for entry" on doors; "please wear your badge" signs
  • "On Deck" table sign near the stage
  • Lunch signs (restaurant, walking time, dietary notes, captain)

docs.title: During the Morning Tutorial
docs.text:
• Costco + HEB supply run: snacks, sodas, misc (ice is ordered online)
  • Late check-ins at the registration desk
  • Check on instructors and A/V periodically
  • Restock at breaks, empty trash

docs.title: End of Day
docs.text:
• Thank instructors
  • Pack leftovers, secure equipment and swag
  • Brief the Saturday team

docs.title: Friday Evening: Appreciation Dinner
docs.text:
Invite-only dinner for speakers, sponsors, organizers, and Friends of PyTexas; there is no separate speaker dinner. Held at a nearby rented space with catering brought in (e.g. a rooftop terrace).

  • Brief speakers in person here (they do not read emails): green room location, on-deck flow, tech-check windows
  • Confirm RSVPs against the headcount given to the caterer

docs.title: Daily Rhythm
docs.text:
• 6:00 venue access
  • Coffee pickup before doors
  • Food delivery before doors (tacos Saturday, kolaches Sunday)
  • 8:00 registration opens; food setup; everything set before doors
  • 8:55 chair sets up opening remarks; sponsor chaser rounds up pitch presenters
  • 9:00 opening remarks (10 min)
  • 9:10 sponsor pitches by tier (Platinum Saturday, Gold/Silver Sunday)
  • 9:20 keynote (~45 min)
  • Talks in 30-minute blocks: 25-minute talk plus 5 minutes of combined Q&A and next-speaker setup
  • 20-minute sponsored talk immediately before lunch (Platinum benefit)
  • Lunch 12:30-2:00, not catered: organizer-led group walks
  • Central Market afternoon-break delivery during the mid-afternoon break
  • Door prizes scattered through the day: after the keynote, before lunch, mid-afternoon, end of day; entry via Google Form
  • Saturday close: sponsored workshop 4:30-6:00, 30 minutes of lightning talks, door prizes, depart for the network event ~6:35
  • Sunday close: lightning talks ~4:45, closing remarks with door prizes ~5:25, cleanup and out by 5:45 (hard out at 7:00)

docs.title: Morning Setup (6:00-8:00)
docs.text:
Registration (2-3 people, doors at 8:00):

  • 3-table bubble layout, room for backpacks
  • 2 laptops on check-in, 1-2 people on badge handout
  • Lanyard stands, swag store, label printer for late adds

Main hall (2-3 people):
