  • Test A/V, mics, confidence monitors, livestream, speaker timer
  • On-deck table with signage near stage
  • Backup dongles (Dell, Apple, HP; USB-C preferred) ready
  • Slido on the control laptop

Catering (1-2 people):

  • Receive delivery 10+ minutes before doors
  • Two food lines, marked clearly (sign or volunteer)
  • Coffee, water and soda coolers, ice
  • Trash in 2+ spots

Streaming and Discord (1 person plus a trained backup):

  • Go live 10-15 minutes early
  • Slido ready for the first session
  • Welcome post in Discord

docs.title: Throughout the Day
docs.text:
Registration desk:

  • Continue check-ins; sales run through the conference with day-of walk-ups
  • Bright loaner lanyards for forgotten badges
  • Day-of paid swag through Pretix voucher QR codes, not cash

Speaker green room:

  • Check the green room before each talk block
  • On-deck speaker seated when the previous talk starts
  • Tech checks catch-as-catch-can between stage events
  • Collect slide backups; water for speakers

A/V (rotate the duty, not one person all weekend):

  • Watch livestream and audio
  • Reset Slido per session, archive after

Catering:

  • Restock at breaks
  • Emergency store runs as needed
  • Track consumption and count leftovers (diet/zero sodas, sparkling water, and fruit are the hits)

Discord:

  • Moderate Slido before questions display
  • Post speaker links and handles as each talk starts
  • Compile every link shared in the conference channel into one doc

Sponsors:

  • Check on sponsors twice daily
  • Photos of sponsor tables

docs.title: Lunch (12:30-2:00)
docs.text:
• Lunch destinations decided and signed before the conference, with a captain per restaurant
  • Restaurant map on a slide before dismissal
  • Captains lead groups; avoid slow venues; check Sunday opening hours
  • Announce the 2:00 resume time

docs.title: End of Each Day
docs.text:
• Thank sponsors and speakers on stage
  • Saturday: announce network event details before the 6:35 departure
  • Pack leftovers; give leftover food to library staff (decided in advance)
  • Secure equipment and swag
  • Daily social recap
  • Brief the next day's team, update the run of show

docs.title: Sunday Teardown (5:25-5:45)
docs.text:
• Organizer huddle, assign teardown
  • Photograph venue property at load-out (also do this at load-in) to avoid disputes
  • Pack everything, clean venue, out by 5:45
  • Final check with library staff, load vehicles

docs.title: Staff Identification
docs.text:
• Organizer shirts in a distinct color from attendee shirts, chosen each year
  • A second distinct style marks the program/speaker team
  • Phone roster lives in the Org Info Sheet; print copies for organizers

docs.title: Networking Event (Saturday Evening)
docs.text:
See network-event.md.

  • Arrive early to coordinate with venue or catering staff
  • Ticket check at the door; waitlist form ready if sold out
  • Welcome and facilitate intros
  • Thank sponsors present
  • Photos
  • Settle bills, coordinate organizer transport

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Registration:

  • App down: use printed backup, sync later
  • Person not in system: try email variations and name search; worst case, blank badge and label printer
  • Bot fails on bulk corporate purchase (registering email vs attendee email): manually add the Discord role

A/V:

  • Projector won't display: try Dell/Apple/HP dongles; USB-C preferred; fall back to the speaker's screen
  • Mic down: hot swap, batteries, A/V vendor
  • Stream drops: library bandwidth dips happen; hotspot failover is impractical, so ride it out and note timestamps for the vendor
  • Timer dies: phone running stagetimer.io

Catering:

  • Delivery late: delay start; always order with a 10+ minute buffer
  • Running short: emergency Costco or HEB run
  • Allergens: signs pre-made, separate trays

Speakers:

  • Late or missing: phone tree, shuffle slots, Python trivia filler
  • Tech broken: backup slides on an organizer laptop
  • Running over: 5/2/wrap warnings, cut Q&A
  • Never let the schedule run early; have filler ready

Venue:

  • Hallway too loud: close doors during talks; sound deadening is a standing open problem

docs.title: Day-of Roles
docs.text:
• Conference Chair: overall coordination, escalations, executive calls
  • Registration Lead: check-in, badge desk, volunteers
  • Speaker Coordinator: green room, on-deck table, tech checks
  • A/V Coordinator: stream, mics, timer, vendor liaison
  • Catering Coordinator: levels, restocks, store runs
  • Discord Moderator: chat, Slido, speaker info posts (with a trained backup)
  • Sponsor Liaison: tables, pitch timing, sponsor chaser duty
  • Swag Coordinator: shirt table, swag store, inventory

docs.title: Emergency Contacts
docs.text:
The phone roster lives in the Org Info Sheet. Before the conference, confirm it covers:

  • All organizer phone numbers
  • A/V vendor emergency line
  • Library facilities and venue emergency
  • Networking event venue or caterer
  • Caterers
  • Local hospital
  • Non-emergency police

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Don't panic at the conference chair until at least day two.
  • Tangled lanyards bottleneck registration; keep them on stands, separate from badges.
  • People miss the second food line; use a sign or a volunteer to direct.
  • People forget badges on day 2; stock bright loaner lanyards.
  • A printed phone roster beats chat tools in emergencies.

docs.title: Day-of Supplies Runbook
docs.text:
The shopping and packing list. Owned by Venue Committee.

See catering.md for the catering plan sheet; the "Who's Getting What" tab there assigns an owner per item.

docs.title: A/V + Tech
docs.text:
• Dongles: Dell, Apple, HP (multiple of each; USB-C preferred)
  • HDMI cables (extra long for stage)
  • Extension cords (10+)
  • Power strips (every tutorial table + registration + stage)
  • Gaffer tape (multiple rolls)
  • Portable label printer (badges for late registrants)
  • Phone chargers (USB-C, Lightning, micro)

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
• Lanyard stands (multiple)
  • Blank badge cardstock (hard stock, ~10% buffer over registrations)
  • Badge holders (~10% buffer)
  • Lanyards (~10% buffer)
  • Bright loaner lanyards for forgotten badges
  • Backup name tag stickers
  • Marker pens (Sharpies)
  • Pens, paper, clipboards
  • Tape, scissors
  • Wire shelves behind registration (deep enough for shirt bags)

Day-of paid swag goes through Pretix voucher QR codes, not cash. See swag.md.

docs.title: Swag
docs.text:
• Poker chips (shirt distribution)
  • Size signs (S, M, L, XL, etc.)
  • Paper bags (shirt bundling)
  • Inventory tracking sheet
  • Ribbons (meetup organizer, hiring, etc.)

docs.title: Catering / F&B
docs.text:
• Allergen labels and signage (pre-print; keep gluten-free and nut-free lines separate)
  • Tongs for snack plates
  • Plates, napkins, utensils
  • Cups (lots of coffee cups, plus lids; both run out fast)
  • Coolers
  • 5-gallon buckets for ice transport
  • Trash bags, plus 2+ trash cans positioned
  • Kettle (people ask for hot water and tea)
  • Sugar, creamer, alternatives
  • Black totes for hauling
  • Chafing dishes
  • Tablecloths (linens rented from American Party Rental; the library provides none)

docs.title: Signage
docs.text:
• Food and allergen signs (pre-printed)
  • Lunch signs (restaurant, walking time, dietary notes, captain)
  • "Badge Required for Entry" door signs
  • "Please Wear Your Badge" signs
  • "On Deck" table sign near stage
  • Sponsor signage, including any sponsored food or coffee table sign per contract
  • Directional signage (plan on the Miro board; check whether the library has sign holders)
  • White posterboard and stencils for ad-hoc signs
  • Lunch captain flags

docs.title: Emergency Kit
docs.text:
• First aid kit
  • Small cash reserve
  • Printed phone roster (from the Org Info Sheet)
  • Spare batteries (mic, timer)
  • Tylenol, Advil

docs.title: Tutorial-Specific
docs.text:
• Power strips at every table (a perennial complaint when missed)
  • Extra extension cords
  • Pre-tested setup instructions for attendees

docs.title: Costco + HEB Run
docs.text:
Runs happen Friday morning during the first tutorial, with restock runs as needed through the weekend. Use prior years' receipts and leftover counts to size quantities; the catering plan sheet carries the actuals.

Calibration from leftover counts:

  • Diet and zero sodas, sparkling water, and fruit are the hits; buy heavy on those
  • Regular sodas linger; buy light
  • Bananas: budget about one per two to three attendees per day (roughly 40-50 lb at full capacity); apples run lighter, with only a bag or two left over
  • Muffins and kolaches tend to get over-ordered; buy fewer
  • Water gets mostly consumed; day 2 uses less water and soda than day 1
  • Buy light Friday to gauge the year's preferences, then bulk-buy for the weekend

Ice: order online. Repeated store runs are the fallback restock mechanism and eat organizer time.

docs.title: Buying Strategy
docs.text:
• Pre-buy reasonable amounts; restock during the conference if needed
  • Unused unopened items can be returned to Costco
  • Remind vendors the 501(c)(3) status removes sales tax

docs.title: Reuse Year Over Year
docs.text:
• Ribbons (extras)
  • Bright loaner lanyards for forgotten badges
  • Signage frames (refresh paper inserts)
  • Coolers, totes, chafing dishes

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Count leftovers each year to recalibrate quantities; the catering plan sheet carries the actuals.
  • Badges run short without a buffer; order ~10% over registrations.
  • Move ice with the 5-gallon buckets, not the scoop.

docs.title: Discord and Hybrid Setup Runbook
docs.text:
Owned by Community Committee.

Community chat and organizer coordination run on Discord, with a webhook feeding ticket purchases into a channel.

See community-committee-runbook.md.

docs.title: Server Prep (Month -8 to -7)
docs.text:
• Archive prior conference channels
  • Create new year channels:
  • Voice channels for networking
  • Roles: Organizer, Speaker, Sponsor, Attendee (in-person), Attendee (virtual), Volunteer
  • Update server icon and banner

docs.title: Bot (Month -8 to -7)
docs.text:
• Pull last year's bot from the repo
  • Confirm a maintainer plus at least one second maintainer; a one-person bot is a single point of failure
  • Develop it like software: changes go through PR review and get demoed at planning meetings
  • Scope slash commands to what will actually exist by conference time: /poll, /question, /schedule first; /icebreaker, /coffee, /intro are nice-to-have
  • Test /register: role assignment, ticket verification, error handling
  • Manual override commands for organizers
  • Document deployment and permissions

The bot is hosted on the PyTexas DigitalOcean account.

Known failure mode: /register fails for bulk corporate purchases because the ticket carries the registering (buyer's) email, not the attendee's. Manual role assignment is the fix; capture both emails at purchase if the ticketing setup allows it.

docs.title: Slido (Month -3 to -2)
docs.text:
• Buy a single-event license
  • One Slido event per talk session or reusable
  • Moderation settings (prevent spam)
  • Archive questions after each talk
  • Mods approve, filter, and mark answered

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Stream to YouTube
  • Coordinate the stream with the A/V vendor
  • Test stream at least one week ahead
  • Go live 10-15 minutes before the first session each day
  • Train at least one backup who knows the full YouTube plus Discord workflow; a solo operator is an illness away from no stream
  • Capture speaker Discord handles in the speaker intake form for direct messaging

docs.title: Captioning
docs.text:
• Confirm captioning with the A/V vendor early; display method and recording behavior take months to settle
  • Slide pre-uploads plus speaker-provided technical-term lists feed caption prep
  • Test before the conference

See av.md.

docs.title: Virtual Attendees
docs.text:
• Define the offering: livestream, Discord access, Slido Q&A, recordings post-conference
  • Welcome email with /register instructions
  • Test stream access before the conference
  • Dedicated channel for virtual attendees

Size expectations honestly: virtual ticket sales are tiny regardless of the cap; expect a handful to a few dozen. All in-person tickets include virtual access.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
• Name the primary chat and stream operator plus at least one trained backup
  • Pick ONE chat tool for day-of organizer coordination; juggling Discord plus Slack plus Slido at once is painful
  • Brief everyone on CoC handling and escalation (see coc.md)
  • Mod-only channel for coordination

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Documented: - /register - verify ticket, assign attendee role

Wishlist (verify what actually shipped before documenting): - /poll, /question, /schedule first - /icebreaker, /coffee, /intro nice-to-have

Moderation runs on manual role assignment and Discord's native moderation tools.

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
/register fails: - Cause: email mismatch, bulk corporate purchase, DB sync issue - Fix: manually assign the Attendee role - Document for bot improvement

User can't find registration: - Try email variations, full name - Check Pretix directly - Escalate to Finance if needed

Bot offline: - Check status, restart - Manual role assignment in the meantime - Contact either maintainer

Virtual attendee can't see channels: - Verify the Virtual role is assigned - Check channel permissions

docs.title: Morning (Each Day)
docs.text:
• Welcome post in #general
  • CoC reminder
  • Start the stream 10-15 minutes early and verify it
  • Slido ready for the first session

docs.title: Per Talk
docs.text:
• Post speaker info as the talk starts: name, LinkedIn or handles, talk title, slides link when available; attendees appreciate these posts
  • Moderate Slido before display
  • Archive Slido after the talk
  • Point overflow Q&A to conference-chat; speakers answer there after their slots

docs.title: Throughout
docs.text:
• Compile every link shared in conference-chat into the link-compilation doc, organized per day
  • Respond to attendee questions
  • Handle /register failures with manual role assignment
  • Welcome and engage virtual attendees
  • Watch for CoC violations (see coc.md)

docs.title: Week 1
docs.text:
• Keep Discord active (highlights, recordings, slides, discussion)
  • Thank moderators

docs.title: After Publishing
docs.text:
• Post recording links per talk
  • Post slide links and the compiled links doc
  • Archive conference channels after 2-4 weeks
  • Maintain general channels year-round

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
• Bot hosted on the PyTexas DigitalOcean account, with a maintainer and a second maintainer
  • Slido: single-event license per conference
  • Speaker headshot storage: use storage the Foundation controls (e.g. a DigitalOcean Spaces bucket); Pretalx-hosted image links rot and break the site

docs.title: Year-Round
docs.text:
• Active server (Python news, discussion, Q&A)
  • Coordinate social with Marketing
  • Highlight community projects
  • Welcome newcomers
  • Pre-conference engagement (countdown, speaker intros, attendee intros)

docs.title: Cross-Committee
docs.text:
• Speaker: speaker info for posts, Discord handles at intake, KBYG covers Slido and Discord
  • Marketing: messaging alignment, social posts
  • Finance: registration issues, opportunity grant announcements
  • Venue: stream coordination with the A/V vendor

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Slido jumps around when questions get reordered; mark or skip answered questions instead of hunting.
  • Slido polls take center stage and block Q&A; run at most one per session.
  • Library bandwidth dips can degrade the stream; hotspot failover is impractical, so ride out drops and note timestamps for the A/V vendor.
  • Don't move chat platforms; Discord works, and switching costs a year of momentum.

docs.title: Attendee Feedback Runbook
docs.text:
Owned by Community Committee, with Marketing promoting the survey and Speaker Committee distributing per-speaker feedback.

See post-event.md for the wider post-conference sequence and community-committee-runbook.md for aftercare.

docs.title: Build (Weeks -2 to -1)
docs.text:
• Build the survey before the conference; it launches on the last day, so it cannot be a post-event task
  • Cover: attendance mode, ratings (overall, organization, pre-event info, keynotes, talks, food, venue, networking event), value-for-ticket, recommend and return scores, free-text favorites and least-favorites
  • Add forward-looking questions the committees actually need answered (format experiments, topic demand, swag interest)
  • Keep it 5-10 minutes; mostly optional questions
  • Draft the distribution email and a Discord post

docs.title: Launch and Collect
docs.text:
• Launch on the last conference day; mention it in closing remarks
  • Send the survey email and post in Discord the same day
  • Reminder at one week; final reminder 2 days before close
  • Response window: about 2 weeks
  • Expect roughly 50 responses; write questions worth 50 careful answers rather than chasing volume

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
• Compile ratings and free-text themes into a summary: strengths, recurring criticisms, action items
  • Share with all committees and the Conference Chair
  • Feed the retro doc; the retro meeting lands within ~2 weeks of the conference

docs.title: Per-Speaker Feedback
docs.text:
• Export Slido Q&A and reactions per talk
  • Merge with feedback-form responses about each talk
  • Compile into a per-speaker feedback doc (a "Speaker Feedback Links" doc in the year's Drive folder works well)
  • Distribute to each speaker in the weeks after the conference

Speakers rarely get usable feedback from conferences; this is cheap and appreciated.

docs.title: What Feedback Drives
docs.text:
Examples of what survey responses change:

  • Complaints about topic monoculture (e.g. too many AI-adjacent talks) feed talk-selection balance for the next cycle.
  • Sponsor tutorials reading as rushed or sales-y feed sponsored-content review standards.
  • Single-track crowding, scarce seating, and hallway-space complaints feed venue and layout planning.
  • Demand for more networking formats (roundtables, breakouts, a women-of-Python gathering, mentoring) feeds Community's format planning.

Carry themes like these into the retro with their year attached so future organizers can judge staleness.

docs.title: Emergency-Contact Data
docs.text:
• Emergency-contact info is collected from attendees at registration intake
  • Delete it after the conference; it exists for day-of safety only
  • Confirm deletion as a post-event checklist item

docs.title: Cross-Committee
docs.text:
• Marketing: survey promotion, feedback-form creation timing (flag it by Week -2; it tends to slip late)
  • Speaker: per-speaker feedback distribution
  • Conference Chair: survey summary feeds the retro

docs.title: Finance Committee Runbook
docs.text:
The Finance Committee owns the budget sheet, sponsorship end to end, registration money and reporting, opportunity grants, the PSF grant, insurance, taxes, and the Foundation's bank accounts.

See budget-planning-template.md, sponsorship.md, registration.md, grants.md.

docs.title: Standing Practices
docs.text:
• One budget sheet per year, owned by the finance lead. Anyone can look; nobody edits without talking to the owner. See budget-planning-template.md.
  • Two bank accounts (Grasshopper Bank and a credit union account). Balances are read aloud at meetings; they never go in shared docs or public pages.
  • Weekly Pretix accounting reports, exported to PDF every Monday from about 14 weeks out through conference week and filed in the year's Finance Reports folder in Drive.
  • Registration stats reported at every planning meeting once sales open: counts per ticket class, shirt pre-orders, revenue against target.
  • The Foundation is a 501(c)(3), which removes sales tax on vendor orders. Remind every vendor; quotes drop once the exemption is applied.
  • Sequence dependent purchases behind the sponsor payment that funds them; for example, hold the lanyard order until the lanyard sponsor pays.
  • Invoice promptly after every commitment and follow up on a schedule; payment chasing stretches into conference week when invoicing lags.
  • Keep every hard payment date in the standing Upcoming Deadlines block of the minutes.

docs.title: Month -12: New Budget
docs.text:
• Create next year's budget sheet during the current conference weekend, ideally on day 1
  • Carry forward last year's structure; review actuals and variance per line
  • Draft targets with the Conference Chair: revenue goal, expense ceiling, profit target

See next-year-planning.md for the parallel venue and dates workstream.

docs.title: Month -8: Kickoff
docs.text:
• Present the budget at kickoff and settle the year's financial goals
  • Review sponsorship tiers against last year's sales and retro notes
  • Confirm ticket classes and rough pricing direction

docs.title: Month -7: Prospectus
docs.text:
• Finalize the sponsor prospectus for publication by early October
  • Publish it and email it to the sponsor mailing list (the per-year Google Group of sponsor contacts), coordinating announcements with Marketing
  • Build the sponsor tracking sheet and start outreach, prior sponsors first

Corporate budget season is the reason for the early-October deadline; slipping past October loses sponsors whose budgets close. Know each prospect's fiscal-year end; deals close when a budget is about to expire.

docs.title: Month -5.5 to -4: Contracts and Ticket Setup
docs.text:
• Clone per-tier sponsor agreement templates from last year
  • Set the ticket timeline with Venue: early bird opens December 1 and closes mid-January
  • Prepare the sponsor invoice template (mid-December)
  • Open the opportunity grant application about 4 months out (late December); see grants.md

docs.title: Month -4.5 to -3: Sales Open, Grant Season, PSF
docs.text:
• Early bird tickets open on Pretix December 1
  • Apply for the PSF grant about 3 months out
  • Pay the venue balance (due about 3 months out)
  • Pay the A/V vendor deposit
  • Start the weekly Pretix accounting reports (about 14 weeks out)

The PSF grant requires a published schedule, links to the Code of Conduct and policies, and a budget, and processing takes about 8 weeks. Apply earlier than feels necessary. External grant freezes happen without warning, and the 8-week lead leaves no slack to absorb one.

docs.title: Week -12 to -8: Early Bird Close and Grant Review
docs.text:
• Early bird ends mid-January; coordinate the countdown campaign with Marketing
  • Chase unsigned sponsor contracts and unpaid invoices
  • Opportunity grant applications close about 8.5 weeks out; review them in a dedicated special meeting the next day, not the regular planning meeting (see grants.md)
  • Confirm catering and dinner-venue deposits with Venue (deposits run about half of each total)

docs.title: Week -8 to -4: Insurance and Fulfillment
docs.text:
• Buy event insurance through The Event Helper. Hard deadline about 4.5 weeks out.
  • Fulfill grants: send emails, send funds, comp tickets, and track each to completion
  • Track sponsor comp-ticket redemption; some sponsors never redeem theirs, and unredeemed comps cause confusion
  • Pay swag, catering, and linens invoices as Venue places orders (orders run Weeks -8 to -2.5)

Keep the insurance deadline headlining the Upcoming Deadlines block every week; it is easy to miss otherwise.

docs.title: Final Two Weeks and Conference
docs.text:
• Chase final sponsor payments; expect this to run into conference week
  • Registration stays open through the conference, including day-of walk-ups; only a sellout closes it
  • Provide headcounts to venue, catering, and the network event, and refresh them as late sales land
  • Day-of paid swag runs through Pretix voucher QR codes, not cash
  • Keep receipts for supply runs, parking, and tips

docs.title: Post-Conference
docs.text:
• Collect and pay final vendor invoices; the final A/V installment lands about 3.5 weeks after
  • Reconcile the budget sheet: actuals per line, bottom line against target
  • Confirm every sponsorship payment landed
  • Prepare tax records for the treasurer (a profitable year means tax work)
  • Thank sponsors with Marketing and start early outreach to satisfied sponsors for next year
  • Feed finance lessons into the retro doc

docs.title: A/V Payment Shape
docs.text: Deposit at booking, an installment or two near the event, and a final installment after. Expect the deposit 3 to 6 months out, an installment in the final two weeks, and the final installment about 3.5 weeks after the conference. Whatever schedule the contract sets, every due date goes in the Upcoming Deadlines block until paid.

docs.title: If Things Go Wrong (Untested Guidance)
docs.text:
None of these playbooks has been exercised; treat them as starting points, not procedure.

  • Sponsor cancels: get it in writing, refund if paid, update the budget sheet, and pull their marketing approvals.
  • Pretix outage at the desk: printed attendee list as backup, manual check-in, reconcile afterward.
  • Budget shortfall: flag it to the Conference Chair immediately; cut variable spend (catering scale, swag extras) before anything speaker- or attendee-facing.

docs.title: Opportunity Grants Runbook
docs.text:
Owned by the Finance Committee. Money should never be the reason someone cannot attend.

Contact: foundation@pytexas.org.

docs.title: How the Fund Is Seeded
docs.text:
• A budget line of a few percent of total expenses (see budget-planning-template.md)
  • Keynote and tutorial honoraria that speakers redirect or donate back; this happens most years, so offer speakers the option rather than assuming
  • Optional grant-focused sponsorships (for example, converting unsold Network Event slots into grant sponsorships)

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
• About 4 months out (late December): open the application Google Form and announce it with Marketing
  • Promote the deadline through mid-February; Marketing runs a grant-deadline campaign
  • About Week -8.5: applications close
  • The next day: review everything in a dedicated special meeting, not the regular planning meeting; treat it as a hard "decision today" agenda so every application leaves with a decision
  • Weeks -8 to -5: notify applicants, disburse funds, comp tickets, and track each grant to completion

docs.title: Application Form
docs.text:
Fields: name, email, total amount requested, itemized expense list, free-text comments.

  • Publish a per-person guidance range on the form; applicants ask for one
  • Design the form so the amount requested reconciles against the itemized expenses
  • Include hotel-booking guidance; downtown Austin is expensive
  • Ask in the CFP whether selected speakers will need travel assistance, so grant demand is visible early

docs.title: Decision Patterns
docs.text:
Apply these consistently at the review meeting:

  • Accepted speakers requesting support are auto-priority.
  • Local applicants asking only for a ticket get a comped ticket through Pretix instead of grant funds; comps do not touch the grant budget and preserve the fund for travel cases. This covers student orgs requesting fees for multiple members too.
  • Large international requests are declined, with a consistent recorded rationale: high cost relative to the fund, regional conferences nearer the applicant, visa responsibility, and applicant safety.
  • A single request equal to the entire fund gets declined.
  • Organizers of peer community conferences can be funded partly as a relationship investment.
  • Flag and merge duplicate applications.

docs.title: Fulfillment Tracking
docs.text:
Work from the responses sheet itself. Add a Decision column, a reviewer-notes column, and three boolean columns, and track every applicant to completion:

  • Email Sent
  • Funds Sent
  • Ticket Sent

docs.title: Day-of and After
docs.text:
• Do not mark grant status on badges; recipients get the same experience as every other attendee.
  • Post-conference: thank recipients, share recordings, invite them into Discord and the meetups, and encourage a future CFP submission.

docs.title: Student Outreach
docs.text: Student outreach is a Marketing workstream, not a grant category; students buy the discounted student ticket class directly. Mass-emailing Texas universities converts poorly; personal engagement at the CS-club and faculty level is the standing approach.

docs.title: Keynote Speaker Runbook
docs.text:
Owned by the Speaker Committee.

See speaker-committee-runbook.md.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
• Month -8 (kickoff, mid-August): open the nomination form
  • End of September: close nominations
  • Early October: organizer election (ranked ballot)
  • Late October: decide the ordered invite list
  • November: outreach down the list
  • By Month -5: keynotes confirmed
  • January: public announcement with the speaker list
  • Feb-Mar: coordinate talks, A/V, travel
  • April: day-of

docs.title: Nominations
docs.text:
Tool: Google Form, opened at the kickoff meeting and closed end of September. The form and its responses live in the year's Drive folder under Speakers. Community nomination generates a more diverse candidate pool than organizer brainstorming alone; promote the form widely.

Form fields: - Nominee name - Contact info if known - Why a great keynote - Topic areas - Links to prior talks/content - Nominator name (optional)

Promote with Marketing: - PyTexas social - Discord - Newsletter - Organizer networks - Python community Slacks

Run 4-6 weeks.

docs.title: Organizer Election
docs.text:
Once nominations close, run a ranked-ballot election among the organizers (Google Form). Each organizer scores every candidate from +2 to -2. Compile the results into a rankings doc with vote scores, then decide the ordered invite list as a team (late October).

The invite order is the plan. Rank the list at least five or six candidates deep; invitations often go several names down before someone accepts.

Criteria: - Speaking experience (quality, stage presence) - Topic relevance - Diversity - Community impact - Availability - Draw factor

docs.title: Discussion
docs.text:
• Review top-ranked
  • Pros/cons
  • Balance (topics, backgrounds, lengths)
  • Backup options
  • Ordered invite list

The standard format is two keynotes, one each day, right after opening remarks (~45 minutes each). A sponsor-funded third slot is possible if a sponsor wants it. Decide the count before outreach.

docs.title: Budget
docs.text:
Keynote benefits typically: - Free conference pass - Honorarium - Travel reimbursement / stipend - Hotel or lodging support (set the limit with Finance before outreach) - Friday appreciation dinner invite - Premium schedule slot

Coordinate with Finance on the keynote budget, honorarium policy, and travel/hotel limits before outreach, so the offer in the invitation is real. Keynoters sometimes redirect or donate back their honorarium; redirected honoraria can seed the opportunity grant fund. See grants.md.

docs.title: Initial Contact (November)
docs.text:
Subject: PyTexas [YEAR] keynote invitation

Hi [NAME],

PyTexas [YEAR] is [DATES] in [CITY]. Expecting [N] attendees.

Your work on [SPECIFIC AREA] would resonate with our audience.

Keynote includes:
- Free pass
- [Travel/hotel]
- [Honorarium]
- 45-minute keynote slot

Open to a brief call to discuss?

[NAME], Speaker Committee, PyTexas Foundation

docs.title: Follow-Up
docs.text:
• Initial: top 3-5 candidates
  • 1 week: follow up if no response
  • 2 weeks: move to next candidate
  • Simultaneous outreach OK, but prepare for multiple yeses
  • Some candidates take weeks to respond; build buffer into the outreach window

Be honest about timeline + backup plans. If they're #2 and #1 hasn't responded, say so.

docs.title: Declines
docs.text:
• Thank graciously
  • Ask for referrals
  • Invite them to attend or submit to CFP
  • Keep on list for future years
  • Move to next ranked candidate

docs.title: Confirming
docs.text:
On verbal/email agreement: - [ ] Send formal confirmation - [ ] Request bio (100-150 words) - [ ] Request hi-res headshot - [ ] Confirm conference dates work - [ ] Tentative title + description - [ ] A/V requirements - [ ] Dietary restrictions - [ ] Travel details for booking

Inform committees: - Marketing: announcement coordination - Finance: travel/hotel booking, honorarium - Venue: A/V requirements, green room - Community: Discord + virtual integration

docs.title: Public Announcement
docs.text:
Coordinate with Marketing for the mid-January speaker-list announcement, while early bird is still open.

Include: - Keynote names + photos - Brief bios - Talk titles if available - Why we're excited - Conference dates reminder - Register link

docs.title: 2-3 Months Out
docs.text:
• Final titles + descriptions
  • Final abstract for site + program
  • Slide template (if offering)
  • A/V needs (screen sharing, video, demos)
  • Book travel + hotel with Finance
  • Send logistics packet

docs.title: 1 Month Out
docs.text:
• Talk finalization reminder
  • Offer tech check (especially remote/hybrid)
  • Confirm arrival + Friday appreciation dinner attendance
  • Friday appreciation dinner details
  • Venue + parking/transit info

docs.title: Week Before
docs.text:
• Final arrival confirmation
  • Speaker lounge/green room location
  • Day-of organizer contacts
  • Final conference schedule
  • Last-minute A/V + accessibility needs

docs.title: Check-In
docs.text:
• Meet keynote on arrival
  • Show green room
  • Walk through speaking room + A/V test
  • Introduce to emcee
  • Water + refreshments
  • Organizer emergency contact

docs.title: During Talk
docs.text:
• Emcee has correct bio + intro
  • A/V standing by
  • Record (with permission)
  • Time warnings
  • Facilitate Q&A if part of format

docs.title: After
docs.text:
• Personal thanks
  • Facilitate hallway conversations
  • Food/coffee access
  • Check needs for rest of day
  • Photos with organizers/attendees (if willing)

docs.title: Week 1
docs.text:
• Thank-you email
  • Photos from their talk
  • Preliminary metrics
  • Ask for feedback
  • Confirm reimbursements in process

docs.title: Recording + Content (with Community)
docs.text:
• Edit and upload
  • Share with speaker before publishing
  • Social promo with tag
  • Add to YouTube + archive

docs.title: Long-Term
docs.text:
• Add to past speakers Google Group
  • Updates about next year
  • Public thanks in wrap-up
  • Future opportunities / advisory consideration

docs.title: Tutorial Crossover
docs.text: Some keynote candidates also work as tutorial instructors. When the invite order is decided, note which declined candidates might take a tutorial instead, and hand them to the tutorial recruiting track (see cfp.md).

docs.title: Resources
docs.text: The nomination form, election form, rankings doc, and campaign planning docs live in the year's Drive folder under Speakers and Marketing.

docs.title: Conference Kickoff Meeting Template
docs.text: Structure for the annual PyTexas conference kickoff meeting. The kickoff happens at Month -8, mid-August, virtual, in the evening.

docs.title: Important Documents
docs.text:
Create the year's Important Documents before the meeting and link them at the top of the agenda:

  • The year's minutes and agenda doc (clone last year's template)
  • The year's Drive folder, with access granted to all organizers
  • The year's budget sheet (created during the previous conference weekend; see next-year-planning.md)
  • The year's retro doc (live from day one)

Also have on hand for reference:

  • Conference dates and venue confirmation
  • Previous year's retrospective and survey results
  • Previous year's data spreadsheets

docs.title: Attendee Management
docs.text:
• Send the calendar invite well ahead of the meeting with the agenda and document links
  • Virtual by default (Discord, Google Meet, or Zoom)

docs.title: Meeting Agenda Template
docs.text:
Copy this into the minutes doc.

Target: 45 minutes. Hard cutoff at 1 hour. Put a timer on each section.

docs.title: 1. Welcome and Introductions (10 Minutes)
docs.text: For each attendee: name, Texas city, job or organization, and a fun fact.

docs.title: 2. Conference Overview (5 Minutes)
docs.text:
• Conference dates and venue
  • Key deadlines already known: CFP opens October 1 (the cycle's first hard deadline), early bird tickets on sale in the fall
  • Anything already booked or signed (venue contract, deposit status)

docs.title: 3. Goals (5 Minutes)
docs.text:
Set 3-4 specific goals for the year and write them into the minutes doc header:

  • Ticket sales target and timeline (standing goal: sell out one month prior to the conference)
  • A specific profit target
  • Meeting discipline itself (stick to the agenda, 45-minute target, 1-hour cutoff)
  • Process goals (runbooks, delegation, documentation)

docs.title: 4. Where We Need Help (15 Minutes)
docs.text:
Walk the committee list, describing what each unit owns, then run a round-robin mapping volunteers to committees: "What do YOU want to do?"

Committee Owns Conference Chair Coordination, meetings, next-year planning, escalation, day-of lead Speaker CFP, talk selection, keynotes, tutorials, schedule, speaker comms Finance Budget, sponsorship, registration money, grants, insurance, taxes Marketing Social campaigns, newsletter, website, design assets Venue Venue relationship, A/V, catering, evening events, swag, badges, registration desk, volunteers Community Outreach, Discord, streaming, virtual experience, aftercare

Record the lead for each committee in the minutes. If a lead position stays open, recruiting a replacement becomes a chair action item.

docs.title: 5. How We Work and Next Steps (10 Minutes)
docs.text:
• Tools: task tracking (Asana), the Drive folder, shared password vault
  • Chat platform confirmation (organizing runs on Discord)
  • Meeting cadence: roughly monthly to start, tightening to biweekly then weekly as the conference approaches
  • Documentation commitment: runbooks are updated as we go
  • Action items with owners: speaker lead drives the CFP launch (due October 1), speaker lead opens the keynote nomination form (due: today; launch the form at the kickoff meeting itself), finance lead readies the sponsor prospectus for early-October publication

docs.title: Within 1 Week
docs.text:
• Distribute meeting notes to all attendees
  • Set up committee communication channels
  • Update the task tracker with initial tasks
  • Confirm access to shared resources for all leads

docs.title: Within 2 Weeks
docs.text:
• Each committee lead schedules their first working session
  • Begin work on kickoff action items

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Update this template with lessons from the meeting
  • Create or update committee runbooks as decisions land

docs.title: Meeting Logistics
docs.text:
• Use a timer for each section; park off-topic discussions
  • Document decisions and action items in real time in the minutes doc
  • Every committee leaves with clear next steps

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• Meeting ends within the 1-hour cutoff
  • All committee leads identified, or recruiting an open lead is an assigned action item
  • Follow-up cadence scheduled before ending

docs.title: Template Notes
docs.text:
For the Conference Chair: review and customize this template 1-2 weeks before the meeting with the current year's dates, goals, and context.

For future years: after each kickoff, update this template with what worked and what dragged.

docs.title: Marketing Committee Runbook
docs.text:
The Marketing Committee owns campaigns, the newsletter, social media, the website, and design assets. Swag ordering belongs to the Venue Committee; Marketing runs the campaigns around it (pre-order pushes, the last-chance shirt campaign).

See swag.md, sponsorship.md, and onboarding-new-lead.md.

docs.title: Channels and Tools
docs.text:
• Mailing list (Mailchimp): the workhorse channel. It drives most ticket sales. Monthly sends, weekly near the event.
  • Social platforms: X, Bluesky, LinkedIn, Mastodon (Fosstodon), Facebook. Hashtag #PyTexasConferenceYYYY.
  • Buffer for post scheduling; export analytics after the event.
  • Canva for assets. Build a reusable campaign brand template early in the cycle; leaving it to the final weeks squeezes every later campaign.
  • Discord for community amplification, plus a one-shot post on Python Discord.
  • Mastodon requires GIFs at 720px minimum. Design assets accordingly.

Channel performance, in short:

  • The mailing list carries ticket sales; social turnout across Mastodon, Bluesky, and LinkedIn is low by comparison.
  • Mass emails to Texas universities do not land; CS-club-level personal engagement works better.
  • Paid LinkedIn ads have been evaluated and rejected; other conferences report poor results at this scale.
  • Social promotion needs to start 3-6 months out minimum without paid ads.

docs.title: Weekly Cadence
docs.text:
Standing content themes between milestone campaigns:

  • Monday: quotes
  • Wednesday: tutorial recording promos
  • Friday: community content

Plus monthly meetup posts, rotating sponsor and Friends of PyTexas content, and holiday posts. Keep a filler-content backlog: historical attendance facts, venue promotion, "what you'll get out of the conference" posts, Texas pride, PSF and Python community ties.

docs.title: Checkpoint Cadence
docs.text: Review campaign status at fixed offsets: 3, 2, and 1 months out; 3, 2, and 1 weeks out; the event; +1 week; +2 weeks.

docs.title: Month -12 to -10: Logo
docs.text:
• Decide approach: commission a designer (current practice) or run a design contest
  • Brief the designer: dates, theme, anniversary context
  • Get variations: full color, B&W, dark mode, SVG, social square, web header
  • Finish before kickoff if possible; the logo blocks swag and website work

docs.title: Month -8 to -7: Kickoff and Planning
docs.text:
• New lead onboarding: read last year's marketing folder, read the last two retros, learn the hard deadlines, write your own expectations doc (see onboarding-new-lead.md)
  • Write the year's marketing planning doc and campaign templates in the year's Drive folder
  • Build the reusable Canva campaign template now, not at Week -3.5
  • Prep the year's website repo so it is live before October 1; the monthly newsletter goes out on the 1st and must link it
  • Self-host the schedule rather than deep-linking into Pretalx, and give speaker headshots a stable home outside the site repo; external deep links rot and break the site
  • Get the logo SVG and dark-mode variant to the website team

docs.title: October 1: CFP Announcement Campaign
docs.text:
CFP opens October 1 (Pretalx) and closes early December.

  • One Mailchimp email
  • Same-day posts on X, Bluesky, LinkedIn, and Fosstodon; LinkedIn gets its own longer copy variant
  • Canva assets in three sizes: Twitter-sized, square, and general 1200x630
  • List the CFP on pythondeadlin.es and the python.org events calendar
  • Offer CFP-writing help via Discord and a how-to blog post
  • Direct CFP invitations to past speakers via the per-year speakers Google Group

Through the CFP window:

  • Reminder posts through the window; mid-window push to Texas meetup lists
  • Prospectus publicity when Finance publishes it (early October, timed to corporate budget season)

docs.title: December 1: Early Bird Launch
docs.text:
• Early bird tickets open December 1 on Pretix; announcement email plus social posts
  • Regular pushes through the window; pace them toward selling out a month early

docs.title: January: Speaker Reveal and Early Bird Close
docs.text:
• Speaker reveal begins January 15 with the "Guess Who" campaign: two posts per speaker, an anonymized teaser built from bio bullets, then a reveal naming the talk, each across five platforms
  • Track per-speaker copy and published-post links in a sheet; it doubles as the campaign to-do list
  • Collect speaker name, socials, and photo at acceptance time; chasing speakers later stalls the reveal campaign
  • Early bird countdown campaign the week before it closes (~Jan 19)
  • Friends of PyTexas coupon codes issued via Pretix
  • Grant deadline pushes until applications close (~Week -8.5)

docs.title: Weeks -8 to -4
docs.text:
• Shirt pre-orders close ~Week -5: run a last-chance campaign the week before; Venue places the order immediately after (see swag.md)
  • Prep sponsor thank-you campaigns per sponsor: one before, one during (the contract obliges one shoutout)
  • Publish the Attendee Know Before You Go (~5 weeks out, with Finance)
  • Send recap-deck data to the A/V vendor early; this item lingers for weeks when left open

docs.title: Weeks -3.5 to -1
docs.text:
• Meetup.com announcement to the four Texas metro meetups (Austin, DFW, Houston, San Antonio)
  • Website freshness pass: the Speak section goes stale after CFP close; check the sponsor page; add a first-time-attendee what-to-bring page
  • Sponsor countdown posts run daily across the final two weeks, one sponsor per slot
  • Build lightning talk signup forms, the feedback form, and the organizer-interest form

docs.title: Conference Days
docs.text:
• Live posts: opening, speaker highlights, sponsor shoutouts, community moments
  • Speaker links get posted in Discord as talks start; one designated operator runs this for the whole conference with at least one trained backup (rotating the duty is impractical given on-site jobs), and Community owns it (see community-committee-runbook.md)
  • End-of-day wrap post each day from a reusable template
  • Photos with permission; back up regularly

docs.title: Week +1 to +2
docs.text:
• Wrap-up posts thanking attendees, speakers, and sponsors
  • Promote the post-event survey (it launches on the last conference day)
  • Export Buffer analytics; file photos in the year's Drive folder
  • Bring marketing lessons to the retro

docs.title: Recordings and the Replay Drip
docs.text:
The recordings pipeline:

  1. The A/V vendor delivers talk videos as unlisted YouTube uploads.
  2. Flip each video public AND flip the playlist public; both steps are needed and one is easy to miss.
  3. Recordings land on pyvideo.org via a manual pull request to the pyvideo/data repo; a single volunteer does this and it is not automated.

Replay drip campaign:

  • One recorded talk promoted per week, every Wednesday, starting ~Month +3 and running ~16 weeks.
  • Five platforms per post, with a GIF per talk (720px minimum for Mastodon).
  • Copy pattern: hashtag replay framing, 2-3 benefit bullets, deep link to the talk on the schedule page.
  • Sponsored talks are marked "(Sponsored)" and included in the rotation.
  • Plan it as a calendar first and write copy second; a sheet tracks per-platform scheduled dates per talk.

docs.title: The Approved To Market Gate
docs.text: Marketing maintains the sponsor marketing sheet: one row per sponsor with tier, copy, and post links. Finance supplies the paid status and the "Approved To Market?" decision. Marketing posts nothing about a sponsor until that column says yes. Unpaid or unconfirmed sponsors never get a post.

docs.title: Cross-Committee
docs.text:
• Finance: paid status and the Approved To Market decision for the sponsor marketing sheet, KBYG docs, ticket pacing data
  • Speaker: speaker data at acceptance (name, socials, photo), schedule for the reveal campaign
  • Venue: swag ordering and the shirt pre-order deadline (Marketing runs the campaigns)
  • Community: meetup amplification, Discord posting, survey distribution

docs.title: Network Event Runbook
docs.text: Venue Committee owns this. Covers both evening events: the Saturday network event (open to attendees as a ticket add-on) and the Friday appreciation dinner (invite-only). See venue-committee-runbook.md and catering.md.

docs.title: Saturday Network Event
docs.text: Saturday evening, about 3 hours (6:00-9:00 PM pattern), roughly 150 guests. Together with food and beverage, this is one of the largest expense categories in the budget.

docs.title: Two Operating Models
docs.text:
Off-site bar buyout. Contract structure: hourly venue buyout plus an hourly food-and-beverage minimum plus 20% gratuity on F&B; non-refundable deposit at signing, balance due at the event, cancellation tiers at 14 days. Bar model: attendees get fixed-value drink tickets (combinable; overages paid by the attendee); organizers monitor the tab during the night and release more tickets if spend is tracking under the F&B minimum. Food: rolling waves of shareable bar food (pizzas, sliders, chips and queso, pretzel bites, brownies); start with a few of everything, reorder as items run out. Pricing is predictable, and the venue handles alcohol compliance.

Self-catered venue (e.g. a rented rooftop). Food is catered in, alcohol is self-supplied (bulk purchase from Costco), and bartenders are hired separately. Self-running alcohol service means the Foundation carries the compliance burden: a TABC permit and a hired licensed peace officer (city requirement; two officers budgeted). Extra logistics: bar tablecloths (two 8-foot), cooler and leftover-alcohol plans, and after-hours venue access coordination.

Default to the buyout model unless there is a strong reason not to; the self-catered model trades venue cost for compliance risk and organizer time.

docs.title: Alcohol Compliance (Self-Run Model Only)
docs.text:
• Submit the TABC permit application months out; approval is slow, and a late submission can still be in review the day before the event
  • Secure a licensed peace officer early; hiring one can take a month of bounced emails and often closes through a personal contact
  • Arrange officer payment logistics in advance, not on the day
  • Plan who buys and transports the alcohol; confirm the bartending vendor's scope in the quote
  • Agree the fallback with the Chair in advance: worst case, no alcohol

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
• Kickoff to Month -6: build the candidate venue list
  • Weeks -11 to -8: get quotes, tour, and book
  • Week -8.5: confirm headcount (~150) and deposit amounts
  • Week -6.5: pay the deposit (roughly half of the total)
  • Weeks -5 to -4: peace officer and TABC work if self-running alcohol (start the officer hunt months earlier)
  • Week -2.5: finalize the event plan
  • Day -1: deliver any marquee or screen content the venue requested

docs.title: Ticketing and Door
docs.text:
• Sell the event as a Pretix ticket add-on; free entry classes exist for sponsors and organizer comps
  • Network Event tier sponsors get a table; their ticket vouchers must be redeemed early to reserve space
  • Check tickets at the door; cover every entrance
  • Stand up a waitlist form on sellout; the standing flow offers either an immediate paid add via invoice, or an email-confirmation option where the org may call 8 AM-6 PM and the person has 4 hours to accept or forfeit
  • The add-on sells close to capacity; expect a waitlist

docs.title: Day-Of
docs.text:
• Arrive 30-60 minutes before doors; brief venue staff, bartenders, and volunteers
  • Set up the door check with the attendee list ready
  • Monitor capacity and the F&B tab (buyout model) through the night
  • Take photos; thank sponsors present
  • Plan leftovers, coolers, and organizer transport home before the event starts
  • Confirm everyone is out, settle bills, and do a final walkthrough with the venue

docs.title: Friday Appreciation Dinner
docs.text:
The Friday dinner is its own institution, distinct from the Saturday event.

  • Invite-only: speakers, sponsors, organizers, and Friends of PyTexas; about 50-75 guests.
  • Venue and caterer are chosen each year (a restaurant private room, a rented rooftop, or a catered alternative venue); a bar is standard.
  • The speaker event and the thank-you dinner are one Friday event; there is no separate speaker dinner.
  • Speakers are briefed in person here (speakers do not reliably read email); the speaker KBYG carries the RSVP-count reminder.

Checklist:

  • Week -11: set the headcount assumption (50-75) in the catering ideas doc
  • Weeks -10 to -8: get quotes at two headcount variants
  • Week -6.5: pay the deposit (roughly half of the total)
  • Weeks -2 to -1: collect dietary restrictions from speakers and guests; the final week is too late
  • Week -1: confirm final headcount from speaker and sponsor RSVPs
  • At the dinner: brief speakers in person on day-of logistics

This is the event that can be nicer than the rest of the catering; it is the thank-you to the people who make the conference run. Dinner catering tends to run over its budget line, so size the budget honestly.

docs.title: Cross-Committee
docs.text:
• Finance: contracts, deposits, add-on ticket pricing, Network Event sponsor tier
  • Marketing: event promotion, sellout and waitlist messaging
  • Speaker: dinner invites and RSVP counts via the speaker KBYG
  • Community: pre-event Discord buildup
  • Conference Chair: sponsor thanks at opening remarks

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• A space can feel cramped at entry even with empty tables further in; walk the room layout before booking.
  • Order for dietary variety as well as volume; vegetarians and non-beef/pork eaters have been left short.
  • Attendees ask for networking earlier in the day; one floated idea is converting Saturday's last two hours to networking/open spaces and running a sponsor-hosted after party where attendees buy their own food and drink.

docs.title: Next-Year Planning Runbook
docs.text:
Owned by the Conference Chair.

Next-year planning is a standing workstream inside the current planning cycle. By the time the current conference ends, next year's dates are announced, the venue contract is signed, the deposit is paid, the budget sheet exists, and the retro doc is live.

See conference-committee-runbook.md, venue.md, post-event.md.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text: Offsets are relative to the current conference (mid-April).

docs.title: Month -6 to -5 (October, November)
docs.text:
• [Chair] Gather venue pricing intel for next year and raise it in a planning meeting; library pricing can jump sharply year over year
  • [Chair] Ask organizers for alternative venue ideas; default is staying at the library if nothing better surfaces

docs.title: Week -11 (Late January)
docs.text:
• [Chair] Choose next year's dates by conflict-checking the Austin events spreadsheet
  • [Chair] Confirm the venue can hold those dates

The spreadsheet tracks Easter, Passover, Texas Relays, Cap10k, the kite festival, SXSW proximity, and graduations. Some conflicts are unavoidable; pick the least bad weekend and note the known overlap in the minutes.

docs.title: Week -10 to -9 (Early February)
docs.text:
• [Chair] Signed next-year venue contract in hand; the standing target is February 1
  • [Chair] Pay the next-year deposit about 9 weeks before the current conference
  • [Chair] Decide scope while booking: which spaces to include (event center, rooftop, demo area); every extra space adds operational overhead

If the contract slips past February, sign immediately after the current conference at the latest. Agreements typically get signed 12-14 months out.

Venue payment structure: a deposit of roughly half the total at signing, with a 14-day return deadline on the signed agreement. The balance is due about 3 months before the event. Cancellation refund tiers step down at 91+, 31-90, and 30 days.

docs.title: Week -8 to -4 (February, March)
docs.text:
• [Chair] Theme brainstorm in a regular meeting (~7.5 weeks out)
  • [Chair] Pick next year's theme and logo direction (~4.5 weeks out)
  • [Chair/Marketing] Line up a graphic designer for the logo; production runs Month -12 to -10 of the next cycle so the logo is done before kickoff
  • [Chair] Confirm next cycle's coordination tooling (organizing runs on Discord with a ticket-purchase webhook)

docs.title: Conference Weekend
docs.text:
• [Finance] Create next year's budget sheet during the current conference weekend, ideally on day 1
  • [Chair] Create next cycle's retro doc; it is live from day one and accumulates all year
  • [Marketing] Announce next year's dates at the current conference; announce with a draft page, do not build the full site during the event

docs.title: Weeks +1 to +2
docs.text:
• [Chair] Countersign and return the venue agreement if not already done; pay the deposit within the 14-day window
  • [Chair] Fold retro action items into the new cycle's planning (see post-event.md)

docs.title: Why This Runs In-Cycle
docs.text: The venue calendar fills more than a year out, and the library's pricing and terms shift year to year. Signing early locks the dates, the rate, and the announcement at the current conference. Waiting until after the conference means announcing "dates TBD" to a room full of attendees who plan travel.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Do not build the full next-year site during the event; announce dates with a draft page and finish the site later.
  • Extra venue spaces look attractive on paper and cost real operational attention on the day; book only what the program needs.
  • The budget sheet and retro doc existing before kickoff is what lets the kickoff run in 45 minutes; see kickoff-meeting.md.

docs.title: Onboarding a New Committee Lead
docs.text: There is no formal chair training program; this checklist is the closest thing that exists. The incoming lead and the Conference Chair build a self-onboarding doc together on their first call. Prior-year artifacts plus the retros are the curriculum.

docs.title: Onboarding Checklist
docs.text:
• Read your area's folder in the prior year's Drive artifacts (Marketing, Networking Event, Speakers, Sponsors, Venue, Run of Show, Speaker Gifts, Swag). The Speakers folder is explicitly marked as reusable as a base for this year; treat the rest the same way.
  • Read the last two retro docs; a single year hides recurring problems.
  • Learn the hard deadlines for your area from the master timeline (CFP opens October 1, prospectus published early October, early bird opens December 1, insurance by Week -4.5, and so on). See conference-master-timeline.md.
  • Write your own expectations doc: what you own, your milestone dates, what you need from other committees, and what you still need to learn. Store it in the year's Drive folder.
  • Get tool access early: shared 1Password, the year's Drive folder, the task tracker, Canva, and anything specific to your area. Check seat and sharing limits; a Miro board can refuse members outside the original team, so either one person owns updates or the board gets duplicated to an account that can share.
  • Give a 5-minute committee update at every planning meeting. The update slot is the accountability mechanism; there is no other check-in.

docs.title: Notes for the Conference Chair
docs.text:
• The kickoff meeting doubles as recruiting: volunteers are mapped to committees round-robin ("what do YOU want to do").
  • Point every new lead at this page plus their role page under ../roles/.
  • If a lead joins mid-cycle, walk them through the Upcoming Deadlines block in the minutes on their first call so nothing hard-dated slips during handoff.

docs.title: Relevant Runbooks
docs.text:
• Kickoff Meeting
  • Conference Master Timeline

docs.title: Post-Event Survey + Retrospective Runbook
docs.text:
Owned by Community Committee (survey) + Conference Committee (retro).

See community-committee-runbook.md, conference-committee-runbook.md.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
• Last conference day: survey launches
  • Days 7-12: survey reminders
  • Week 2: close survey + compile data; retrospective meeting
  • Week 2-3: action items + runbook updates; distribute per-speaker feedback

The retro doc is not created after the event. It exists from day one of the cycle and accumulates all year; the retro meeting reviews it alongside the survey data. See next-year-planning.md.

Do the retro within 2 weeks while it's fresh. Don't skip.

docs.title: Setup (Before Conference)
docs.text:
Build in Google Forms.

Sections: - Overall (NPS-style + rating) - Talks - Venue - Food - Registration process - A/V - Virtual experience (if virtual ticket) - Discord/community - Networking event - Improvements - Open feedback

Keep it 5-10 minutes max. Mix rating + open-ended. Most questions optional.

Consider drawing for swag to lift response rate.

docs.title: Distribution
docs.text:
Launch on the last conference day, not days later: - Announce during closing remarks - Email to all attendees - Discord post - Social mention

Reminders: - Day 7: reminder - Day 12: final reminder - Day 14: close

Responses come in over about 2 weeks; expect roughly 50.

docs.title: Survey Email
docs.text:
Subject: Quick PyTexas [YEAR] survey

Hi [NAME],

Help us make next year better.

[SURVEY LINK]

5-10 minutes. [INCENTIVE if used].

Covers: experience, talks, venue, food, what to improve.

Closes [DATE].

The PyTexas [YEAR] Team

docs.title: Analysis (Weeks 2-3)
docs.text:
• Close survey
  • Quant data: average ratings per category
  • Qual data: themes from open-ended
  • Standout positive comments
  • Standout negative comments
  • Compare to last year if data available

docs.title: Summary Document
docs.text:
• Overall satisfaction score
  • Category breakdowns
  • Strengths
  • Improvements
  • Specific action items
  • Demographic breakdown of respondents

Share with: - All committees - Conference Chair - Foundation Board

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
Hold within 2 weeks of conference. Single meeting, 2-3 hours.

Attendees: all organizers + key volunteers.

Format: 4 columns.

  1. What Went Well
  2. What Went Poorly
  3. What New Ideas Do We Have
  4. What Actions Will We Take

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Review and organize the cycle's retro doc; it accumulates well/poorly/ideas notes all year, so sort it into the four columns before the meeting
  • Share survey results
  • Send pre-meeting note: "Add anything you want to discuss"
  • Calendar 2-3 hours

docs.title: Running the Meeting
docs.text:
Per section (allocate ~30 min each): - Round-robin contributions - Discussion of patterns - Capture in doc

Action items in section 4: - Specific - Owner assigned - Target date or runbook to update

docs.title: Follow-up
docs.text:
• Share retro doc with foundation board
  • Update runbooks with action items
  • Archive previous year retro
  • Open issues / Asana tasks for action items

docs.title: Retrospective Template
docs.text:
# PyTexas [YEAR] Retrospective

Date: [DATE]
Attendees: [LIST]

## What Went Well

- [Item] - [optional: who/what made it work]

## What Went Poorly

- [Item] - [optional: root cause]

## What New Ideas Do We Have

- [Idea] - [optional: who proposed]

## What Actions Will We Take

- [ ] [Action] - [Owner] - [Target]
- [ ] Update [runbook].md with [lesson]

## Survey Snapshot

- Overall satisfaction: [SCORE]
- Top strength: [ITEM]
- Top concern: [ITEM]
- Response count: [N]

docs.title: Categories to Cover
docs.text: In both survey + retro: - Registration + check-in - Food + beverage - A/V + livestream - Discord + Slido - Speakers + on-deck - Sponsors - Venue + setup - Networking event - Volunteers - Marketing - Run of show + timing - Day-of communications

docs.title: Cross-Committee
docs.text:
Run committee-specific mini-retros first if useful: - Each committee discusses internally - Surface top 3 wins + top 3 issues - Bring to all-hands retro

Each committee chair owns their committee's runbook updates.

docs.title: Sample Action Items
docs.text: The shape a good action item takes: - Integrate intake form into Pretix ticket purchase (Finance) - Order ice online (Venue) - Count leftovers and pre-plan supply quantities from past years (Venue) - Update runbooks at start of new planning year (all) - Reword the "where did you hear about us" survey question to say "this year" (Marketing) - Phone numbers document (Conference)

docs.title: Sponsor + Speaker Surveys (Optional)
docs.text:
Standing practice covers the attendee survey and per-speaker feedback only. If a year wants to add sponsor or speaker surveys, send separate, shorter ones: - Sponsors (5 min) - Speakers (5 min)

Sponsor questions: - Satisfaction with deliverables - Visibility ROI - Booth traffic - Renewal intent - What would make sponsoring better?

Speaker questions: - Communication clarity - KBYG usefulness - Tech check + on-deck table - Green room experience - Recording quality - Will you submit again?

docs.title: Per-Speaker Feedback
docs.text:
The Speaker Committee compiles Slido data and attendee feedback-form responses into a per-speaker feedback doc and sends each speaker their own feedback. Speakers value it, and it feeds their future CFP submissions.

  • [Speaker] Export Slido Q&A and poll data per talk
  • [Speaker] Pull talk-specific comments from the feedback form
  • [Speaker] Compile links per speaker and email each speaker their set

docs.title: Post-Event Content Pipeline
docs.text:
Pointers only; Marketing and Community own the details.

  • Replay drip campaign: one recorded talk promoted per week starting around Month +3 and running ~16 weeks. See marketing-committee-runbook.md.
  • Recordings land on pyvideo.org via a manual pull request to the pyvideo/data repo (single volunteer, not automated). See community-committee-runbook.md.
  • YouTube publishing: the A/V vendor delivers unlisted videos; each video and the playlist must be flipped public. See av.md.
  • Export Buffer analytics and file event photos in the year's Drive folder.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Stale retros lose detail; hold the meeting within 2 weeks, no exceptions.
  • Action items without owners and dates do not happen.
  • Runbooks are the deliverable; update them while the retro is fresh, not next cycle.

docs.title: Registration Runbook
docs.text:
Owned by the Venue Committee; Finance owns the money side and the weekly reporting.

See venue-committee-runbook.md and day-of-operations-guide.md.

docs.title: Platform: Pretix
docs.text:
pretix.eu. Open source, flexible tiers, good export.

Payments run through Stripe only. Sponsors additionally pay by EFT or purchase order; attendees do not.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
• Month -5.5 to -5 (November): Pretix setup, including demographic questions
  • December 1: early bird opens
  • Week of January 7: speaker list published, drives early bird signups
  • Mid-January: early bird closes, regular opens
  • Through the conference: regular registration stays open, including day-of walk-ups
  • Only a sellout closes registration; some years sell out weeks early and some never do

docs.title: Early Bird
docs.text:
• Period: Dec 1 to mid-January
  • See the budget sheet for pricing
  • Cap each early bird class (individual and corporate) to create urgency

docs.title: Regular
docs.text:
• Period: from early bird close through the conference, including day-of
  • See the budget sheet for pricing
  • Capacity minus early bird sales

docs.title: Student
docs.text:
• Discounted class, .edu email or student ID upload
  • Money should never be a reason someone doesn't attend
  • Available throughout registration

docs.title: Virtual
docs.text:
• Streaming access
  • Demand is small: expect a few dozen sold or comped at most, far below any cap
  • Meetup organizers get free virtual tickets
  • All in-person tickets include virtual access

docs.title: Corporate
docs.text:
• Corporate ticket classes plus bulk packages (10+ at a corporate discount)
  • No sponsor benefits attached; logos and thank-you slides belong to sponsor tiers
  • Works as a foot in the door for companies without sponsorship budgets; track buyers for next year's sponsor outreach

docs.title: Opportunity Grants
docs.text: Handled by Finance. See grants.md. Grant recipients get comped tickets through Pretix.

docs.title: Pretix Setup
docs.text:
• Ticket types + pricing
  • Quantities + limits
  • Early bird end date (mid-January)
  • Required fields:
  • Name, email
  • Company/affiliation (optional)
  • T-shirt size (required for shirt buyers)
  • Dietary restrictions
  • Accessibility needs
  • Pronouns (optional)
  • How heard about PyTexas
  • Demographic questions: source the field list from the Registration Intake form in the year's Drive folder rather than inventing a new set
  • Email confirmation templates
  • End-to-end test
  • Stripe payment processing
  • Admin access for committee

Demographic data informs future planning and feeds the next prospectus. The day-of Registration Intake form is the demographics instrument today; the standing goal is folding it into Pretix so attendees answer once at purchase.

Coordinate launch announcements with Marketing. Coordinate pricing + refund policy with Finance.

docs.title: Launch (December 1)
docs.text:
• Open early bird in Pretix
  • Test purchase flow
  • Social media (with Marketing)
  • Newsletter
  • Discord + community channels
  • Monitor for issues

Push sales earlier and harder than feels necessary; sell-out-early goals slip when the push starts late.

docs.title: Week of January 7
docs.text:
Publishing speakers drives early bird sales.

  • Marketing launches speaker announcements (reveal mid-January, typically with a teaser series)
  • Highlight the early bird deadline
  • "Last week of early bird" countdown
  • Share speaker bios + abstracts

docs.title: Mid-January: Early Bird to Regular
docs.text:
• Close early bird in Pretix
  • Open regular pricing
  • Update site
  • Social announcement
  • Thank early bird purchasers publicly

docs.title: Through Conference
docs.text:
• Weekly sales monitoring; Finance files the weekly Pretix accounting report every Monday
  • Export attendee data 2 weeks out for badge printing
  • Pre-conference emails (Community)
  • Capacity planning with Venue; the sell-out number is 250 in-person, stretchable to 275
  • Keep registration open; only a sellout closes it

docs.title: Data Exports
docs.text:
Schedule: - 2 weeks before: initial for badge printing - 1 week before: update for late adds - Day before: final for on-site materials - Day-of: real-time via Pretix admin

Fields needed: - Name (badge) - Email (comms) - Shirt size (swag) - Dietary (catering) - Accessibility (venue) - Ticket type

Share with: - Finance: revenue, corporate buyers, grant recipients - Venue: headcount, dietary summary, accessibility - Swag Lead: shirt size distribution - Catering: dietary breakdown

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Name (large, readable)
  • Company/affiliation if provided
  • Pronouns if provided
  • Ticket type indicator (color?)
  • PyTexas logo + year
  • Sponsor logos if applicable

Accessibility: large font, high contrast, clear hierarchy.

Choose sturdy cardstock.

docs.title: Print Timeline
docs.text:
• Export Pretix list
  • Order from ConferenceBadges.com (template, print-ahead plus day-of)
  • Stock blank badges and a label printer for walk-ups and late registrants

Badges tend to slip late; order them well before the final two weeks. Expect one more export for late sales since registration stays open.

docs.title: Lanyards
docs.text:
• Lanyard sponsor provides branded
  • conferencebadge.com
  • Office supply (Staples, Office Depot)
  • Reuse from prior years if good

Order 10-15% extra for buffer.

docs.title: Day-of Setup
docs.text:
See day-of-operations-guide.md for the full Friday/Saturday/Sunday flow.

Highlights: - 2 on check-in laptops, 1-2 on badges - 3-table bubble layout with room for attendee backpacks - Organize pre-printed badges alphabetically - Lanyards on a stand, separate from badges (not piles!) - Test the label printer before doors - Everything set by 8:00 exactly - Registration hours: Friday 9-12 and 2-5; Saturday and Sunday from 8:00 - Communication: shared channel

Keep the desk staffed constantly for late-comers and questions.

docs.title: Check-in Flow
docs.text:
Three stations, each with a printed numbered sign:

  1. Scan the QR code and complete the Registration Intake form; show the confirmation screen. The intake form is the demographics instrument that feeds next year's prospectus.
  2. Badge pickup on showing the Step 1 confirmation.
  3. Shirt pickup by poker chip redemption (chips are issued as shirt-entitlement tokens at purchase).

A fourth sign advertises the Discord community.

Walk-ups: 1. Purchase in Pretix on the spot (registration stays open unless sold out) 2. Complete the intake form 3. Blank badge plus label printer 4. Continue the normal flow

Day-of paid swag runs through Pretix voucher QR codes, not cash.

docs.title: Common Issues
docs.text:
• Name not found: check spellings, search by email, check refund/cancel list
  • Badge printed wrong: reprint at station or marker fix
  • Shirt size out: offer to mail, offer alternative, document
  • Forgot confirmation: look up by name/email, verify identity, check in

docs.title: Virtual Attendees
docs.text:
Virtual demand is small, a few dozen tickets at most against a much larger cap. Size virtual effort accordingly.

  • Streaming link emailed
  • Optional virtual swag (see swag.md)
  • Discord access

Setup: - Separate Pretix ticket type - Automated email with streaming instructions - Pre-conference test email (verify link works)

Post-registration: - Export virtual emails for streaming platform - Consider shipping shirts - Discord invites

docs.title: Post-Conference
docs.text:
• Export final attendee list to Drive
  • Actual vs expected attendance
  • No-show rate
  • Post-conference survey (with Community)
  • Revenue numbers to Finance, document fees, refunds, projection vs actual

docs.title: Cross-Committee
docs.text:
• Finance: pricing, revenue, refund policy, corporate strategy, grant ticket allocation
  • Marketing: launch announcements, deadline reminders, social campaigns
  • Speaker: speaker comp tickets, speaker list timing, speaker guest tickets
  • Venue: headcount for catering, accessibility, desk location
  • Swag Lead: shirt size data, distribution

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
• Pretix Docs
  • The year's budget sheet and registration artifacts live in the year's Drive folder

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Shirts are a paid pre-order add-on redeemed by poker chip. Say loudly whether a shirt comes with the ticket; attendee confusion recurs.
  • Ticket messaging must state which days each ticket covers; attendees without tutorial tickets show up Friday when the site advertises a three-day range.
  • The Discord bot fails on bulk corporate purchases (registering email vs attendee email). Have a manual role override ready.

docs.title: Run of Show Runbook
docs.text:
Owned by Conference Chair (with Speaker and Venue committees).

A draft pitch-slot skeleton must exist before the prospectus ships (Month -7) so pitch slots can be written into sponsor contracts. The final grid gets built about 2 weeks out. Left alone it slips to 3-4 days out, and every retro complains; start earlier.

See speaker-committee-runbook.md, day-of-operations-guide.md.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Minute-by-minute schedule the team uses to execute the conference. Lives in a spreadsheet. Updated through the final week.

docs.title: Two Documents, Two Deadlines
docs.text:
1. Pitch-slot skeleton (Month -7, before the prospectus ships): which tiers pitch when, sponsored talk placement, workshop slots. This is what sales writes into contracts.
  2. Final grid (~2 weeks out): every time slot, every lane, built from last year's sheet.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
One sheet, one grid per day (Friday, Saturday, Sunday).

Columns: Time, Duration, Action, Registration/Hallway, Outside Work, Main Hall, Speaker, Notes.

The three role columns (Registration/Hallway, Outside Work, Main Hall) are parallel lanes so hallway staff, errand runners, and stage crew each see their own tasks at every time slot.

Recurring tasks embedded in the lanes:

  • Check the green room before each talk block
  • Check on sponsors twice daily
  • Food setup and teardown around breaks
  • Coffee pickup and urn return
  • Catering arrival windows (breakfast before doors, afternoon during the mid-afternoon break; set exact times with each vendor per year)
  • Store runs (Friday Costco + HEB trip during the morning tutorial)

docs.title: Sponsor Pitch Slots
docs.text:
• Pitches by tier: Platinum pre-keynote Saturday, Gold/Silver Sunday, Bronze during Saturday lightning talks
  • A 20-minute sponsored talk sits immediately before lunch (Platinum benefit)
  • Space pitches through the day; do not cluster
  • Coordinate with Finance on ordering; a sponsor chaser rounds up presenters each morning
  • Lock pitch slots before selling new sponsorships

docs.title: Sample Saturday
docs.text:
6:00  Venue access, setup begins
7:15  Coffee pickup
7:30  Food delivery
8:00  Registration opens, food out
8:55  Chair sets up opening; sponsor chaser rounds up presenters
9:00  Opening remarks (10)
9:10  Sponsor pitches, Platinum (2 min each, per the prospectus)
9:20  Keynote (~45)
10:05 Break + door prizes
10:20 Talk blocks: 25-min talk + 5-min Q&A/next-speaker setup
...   (breaks of 10-15 min interleaved)
12:05 Sponsored talk (20) + door prizes
12:30 Lunch: organizer-led group walks
2:00  Talks resume
2:25  Central Market afternoon delivery window
...
4:30  Sponsored workshop (90)
6:00  Lightning talks (30) + door prizes
6:35  Depart for network event

Sunday differs at the close: lightning talks ~4:45, closing remarks with door prizes ~5:25, out by 5:45.

docs.title: Door Prize Drawings
docs.text: Spread through the day: after the keynote, before lunch, mid-afternoon, end of day. Entry via Google Form. Scattered drawings beat a single end-of-day block.

docs.title: Distribution
docs.text:
• Print copies for organizers, per day
  • Digital link in the organizer chat
  • A/V vendor gets a copy

docs.title: Final Updates
docs.text:
Week before:

  • Confirm all speakers on slot
  • Final sponsor pitch ordering
  • Lunch announcements and restaurant map slide
  • Door prize plan
  • Sponsor thank-you slides ordered
  • Prep last-day slides (announcements, recap) before day-of

Day before:

  • Print run of show per organizer
  • Brief team on changes

Each morning:

  • Confirm changes from the previous evening
  • MC has accurate intros and sponsor mentions
  • Speaker timer set up per session

End of each day:

  • Update the next day's grid based on adjustments
  • Distribute the updated version

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Never let talks run early; it wrecks planned arrivals in person and online.
  • Keep Python trivia or other filler ready for talks that run short.
  • The pitch skeleton must exist before sponsorships are sold.

docs.title: Speaker Committee Runbook
docs.text:
The Speaker Committee owns the CFP, talk and keynote selection, tutorials, the schedule, speaker communications, and day-of speaker coordination.

See cfp.md, keynote.md, run-of-show.md, and conference-master-timeline.md.

docs.title: Month -12 to -8: Before Kickoff
docs.text:
• Recruit tutorial presenters by direct invitation, starting with hallway conversations at PyCon US (~11 months out)
  • Review last year's CFP outcomes and topic gaps
  • Read the last two retros for speaker-related action items
