Tutorials are recruited by direct invitation, not through the open CFP. Plan on two community presenters plus a possible sponsored workshop. Aim to confirm the first tutorial presenter in person at PyCon, eleven months out.

docs.title: Month -8 (Mid-August): Kickoff
docs.text:
• Open the keynote nomination form (Google Form) at the kickoff meeting
  • Set the CFP open date (October 1) as the cycle's first hard deadline
  • Set the rest of the CFP timeline: close early December, review at least 2 full weeks over the holidays, notify around the new year

docs.title: Month -7 (September): CFP Prep
docs.text:
• Update CFP questions in Pretalx: title, abstract, description, level, length, bio, photo, requirements, recording consent, CoC agreement
  • Add a travel-assistance question (feeds opportunity grant planning; see grants.md)
  • Test submission end-to-end
  • Line up reviewers and brief them on the rubric and deadlines
  • Prepare the past-speaker CFP invitation (a per-year Google Group of past speakers exists for this)
  • Coordinate announcement graphics and copy with Marketing
  • Close keynote nominations end of September

docs.title: Month -6.5 (October 1): CFP Opens
docs.text:
• Open the CFP in Pretalx
  • Send direct invitations to the past-speaker Google Group
  • Announce with Marketing: newsletter, social, Discord, python.org events, pythondeadlin.es
  • Run the keynote organizer election (ranked ballot, each candidate scored +2 to -2)

The CFP runs October 1 to early December, a 9-10 week window. A short extension is an option if volume is low near the deadline. Expect a few dozen submissions.

docs.title: Keynote Invite Order
docs.text:
• Compile election results into a rankings doc and decide the ordered invite list (late October)
  • Work down the list in order; be ready to go deep

Invitations often go several names deep before someone accepts. The ranked backup list is the plan, not a contingency. See keynote.md for outreach mechanics.

docs.title: Month -5 to -4: CFP Close and Review
docs.text:
• Mid-window reminder push with Marketing; final-week countdown before close
  • Close the CFP early December
  • Reviewers vote in Pretalx over at least 2 full weeks
  • Hold an in-person decision meeting to pick the lineup and build an ordered waitlist
  • Send the speaker information form to accepted speakers at acceptance time (mid-December): name, socials, photo, logistics

Target roughly 14 talks for the single track and keep an ordered waitlist of about 10 with the top few flagged.

Collect speaker name, socials, and photo at acceptance, not later. Response rates crater once the acceptance moment passes, and Marketing will need the data before speakers get around to it.

docs.title: Month -3.5 (Around January 1): Notifications
docs.text:
• Send acceptances with a hard confirmation deadline (~2 weeks)
  • Keep the waitlist ordered with the top candidates flagged
  • Reject everything below the waitlist promptly
  • Offer standby speakers free tickets
  • Hand speaker data to Marketing for the reveal campaign (~January 15)

Give Marketing the actual headshot and schedule files, never links into Pretalx; those links break later and take the site down with them.

Late dropouts happen even after the schedule is final, sometimes just weeks before the conference. Hold ordered alternates and keep slack in the schedule.

docs.title: Week -11 to -7: Schedule
docs.text:
• Confirm all tutorials
  • Build the draft schedule: 30-minute blocks (25-minute talk plus 5 minutes of combined Q&A and next-speaker setup), keynote (~45 minutes) after opening remarks, a 20-minute sponsored talk right before lunch
  • Slot sponsor pitches with Finance (by tier, spaced across the days)
  • Present the proposed schedule to the organizers (~Week -8)
  • Publish the schedule (the PSF grant application requires a published schedule; see finance-committee-runbook.md)
  • Get Slido and StageTimer single-event quotes (~Week -7.5)

Remote talks are high-risk; an audio failure on one draws more criticism than anything else in the program. If you accept one, rehearse it end-to-end with the A/V vendor and hold a standby talk.

docs.title: Week -2 to -1: Final Prep
docs.text:
• Send the speaker KBYG (~2 weeks out): slot, Discord speaker role, slide upload, tech-check windows, green room, Friday event details
  • Open the slide-upload Drive folder; ask each speaker for a text file of technical terms to feed caption prep
  • Stage backup dongles (Dell, Apple, HP); USB-C is the preferred connection
  • Build per-day lightning talk signup forms (8-9 slots per day)
  • Confirm the speaker RSVP count for the Friday appreciation dinner with Venue

Lightning talk submissions exceed slots every year; organizers curate an ordered subset from each day's form.

docs.title: Friday
docs.text:
• Run speaker tech checks before 9:00 or at lunch (catch-as-catch-can between stage events on the weekend)
  • Greet tutorial instructors and verify rooms: power strips at every table, projection, mic
  • Check in on tutorials during breaks; thank instructors at end of day
  • Evening: Friday appreciation dinner (speakers, sponsors, organizers, Friends of PyTexas); brief speakers in person here

Speakers don't read emails. The KBYG is a reference; the in-person Friday briefing is the real briefing.

Tutorial rooms need power strips at every table; presenters notice when they're missing.

docs.title: Saturday and Sunday
docs.text:
Morning:

  • Set up the on-deck table with signage near the stage

Throughout:

  • Speaker check-in on arrival with a walkthrough (slot, on-deck rule, mic, timer)
  • On-deck rule: the next speaker sits at the table when the prior talk begins; tech check during the 5-minute changeover
  • Time warnings via StageTimer; Q&A via Slido
  • Never run early; keep Python trivia ready as filler
  • Run lightning talks from the day's form (Saturday before close, Sunday ~4:45)

docs.title: Week +1 to +2

  • Collect remaining slides (respect opt-outs)
  • Check recording quality with the A/V vendor

docs.title: Sponsorship Runbook
docs.text: Owned by the Finance Committee. All sponsor contact runs through sponsorship@pytexas.org. See finance-committee-runbook.md for the full finance lifecycle and run-of-show.md for pitch-slot scheduling.

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text:
• Month -7 (September): finalize the prospectus so it publishes by early October. Corporate budget season is the reason; slipping past October loses deals.
  • Month -7: confirm a draft run of show with pitch-slot skeleton exists before the prospectus ships, so pitch slots can be written into contracts. See run-of-show.md.
  • Month -6.5 (early October): publish the prospectus and email it to the year's sponsor Google Group.
  • Month -5.5 (late October): clone per-tier contract templates from last year into the year's Sponsor Templates folder in Drive.
  • Month -4 (mid-December): prepare the year's invoice template.
  • October through conference: run outreach, contracts, invoicing, and payment chasing continuously. Review per-sponsor status at every planning meeting.
  • Week -5: publish the Sponsor KBYG and build the sponsor marketing sheet with the Approved To Market gate.
  • Weeks -2 to 0: sponsor countdown posts run daily (Marketing executes; Finance supplies the approved list).
  • Conference week: chase final payments. This reliably runs into conference week; plan for it.
  • Post-conference: thank-yous, comp-ticket redemption check, renewal outreach.

docs.title: Tier Structure
docs.text:
The prospectus sells four standard tiers and four specialty tiers. Quantities are caps, not targets.

Tier Available Distinguishing benefits Platinum 2 4 tickets plus 10 discounted corporate tickets, pre-keynote pitch Saturday, premium table placement, 20-minute sponsored talk right before lunch Gold 5 2 tickets plus 5 discounted corporate tickets, short pitch Saturday, sponsor-hall table Silver 5 1 ticket plus 2 discounted corporate tickets, short pitch Sunday, back-of-hall table Bronze/Community 15 1 ticket, 1-minute pitch during Saturday lightning talks, popup banner option Lanyard 2 Logo on the conference lanyard Captioning 2 Logo on all-day captioning and on the permanent talk videos Food/Coffee 3 Logo at food tables for one day or the coffee bar both days Network Event 4 Table at the Saturday evening event

Also sold: bulk corporate ticket packages (10+ at a corporate discount). These work as a foot in the door for companies without a sponsorship budget; track buyers for next year's outreach.

Every sponsor at every tier gets: a social media callout, website logo, morning thank-you slide, space on the shared swag table, and a job-board posting.

The Platinum sponsored talk is subject to the normal review process. Sales pitches are rejected, and the prospectus says so explicitly; accepting them risks the Foundation's 501(c)(3) status.

Booth assignment is first come, first served within tier placement rules. Watch table space in the sponsor hall as the count grows. A specialty tier can be invented mid-cycle when a specific cost needs covering; a benefit like captioning can be split across two sponsors. Do not offer a paid hourly demo space; it does not sell.

docs.title: Prospectus
docs.text:
• Rebuild from last year's deck: tiers, benefits, quantities, process.
  • Update demographics slides from last year's registration intake data.
  • Include the check-in rate; PyTexas runs well above the community-event norm and it sells.
  • Confirm pitch slots against the run of show draft before printing benefits.
  • Finance reviews, Conference Chair approves.
  • Publish by early October, save to the year's Drive folder, and email the sponsor Google Group.

docs.title: Recruitment
docs.text:
Past sponsors renew at the highest rate; start there.

  • Email past sponsors through the year's Google Group with a short personalized note and the prospectus.
  • Create next year's Google Group of sponsor contacts as contacts appear.
  • Publish an employee template letter in the newsletter so community members can pitch their own employers.
  • Know each prospect's fiscal-year end and time the ask to it; deals close when a budget is about to expire.
  • Post the prospectus on LinkedIn and the Foundation's accounts (low conversion; still worth the presence).

Companies that have sponsored, as target-list context: Microsoft, Temporal, Anaconda, Elastic, Cloudflare, Bloomberg, GitButler, uStudio, Caktus Group, Black Python Devs, devIT, and Pretix. The PSF grant is treated as sponsorship revenue in the budget; see grants.md. Expect long pursuits that go nowhere; a prospect can be worked for months and still decline.

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text:
• Clone per-tier agreement templates from last year (~5.5 months out): one per standard and specialty tier.
  • Send through Docusign; the Secretary signs first.
  • A countersigned contract is required before anything else moves.
  • Create a per-sponsor folder in the year's Drive Sponsors folder for the contract and invoices.

Contract terms that matter in practice:

  • Payment is net 30 from the effective date.
  • Benefits are secured only on full payment.
  • The Code of Conduct binds sponsor representatives.
  • The Foundation holds a unilateral reputational-risk termination clause.
  • Materials deadlines and booth assignment rules live in the tier exhibit.

docs.title: Invoicing and Payment
docs.text:
• Invoice from the year's template immediately after countersignature.
  • Payment options: Stripe credit card, EFT, or purchase order.
  • Track per-sponsor status at every meeting: contract state, invoice sent, paid.
  • Follow up on unpaid invoices every meeting until closed.
  • Sequence dependent orders behind payment; for example, hold the lanyard order until the lanyard sponsor pays.
  • Track that sponsors actually redeem their comped tickets; some never do, and unredeemed comps cause confusion.
  • Remind sponsors to redeem ticket vouchers early if they want Network Event space.

Payment chasing runs into conference week. Budget standing time for it and never let a benefit ship ahead of the money.

docs.title: Approved to Market Gate
docs.text:
Sponsors get zero promotion until payment is confirmed.

  • Build the sponsor marketing sheet (~5 weeks out): one row per sponsor with tier, paid status, an "Approved To Market?" column, logo, canned promo copy, scheduled post date, and per-platform post links.
  • Marketing posts only rows with the approval flag set. An unpaid sponsor simply never gets a post.
  • The contract obligates one social shoutout; practice is one before the conference and one during.
  • Schedule countdown posts across the final two weeks, one sponsor per slot.

docs.title: Sponsor Know Before You Go
docs.text:
Publish about 5 weeks out to every signed sponsor. Contents that must be in it:

  • Venue address, parking, and Wi-Fi.
  • Check-in windows: Friday morning and afternoon, or Saturday 7-9 AM.
  • Exhibit hours and teardown flexibility.
  • Booth spec: 5-foot table, two chairs, power.
  • Shipping: ship to your hotel; the venue accepts no deliveries.
  • No lead scanners; point to lead-gathering alternatives.
  • Shirt-order deadline (~5 weeks out) for guaranteed day-of pickup.
  • Meals: breakfast provided, lunch on your own.

docs.title: Day-Of
docs.text:
• Assign a sponsor liaison for the weekend.
  • Put a "sponsor chaser" in the run of show each morning to round up pitch presenters before opening remarks.
  • Check on sponsors twice daily (also in the run of show).
  • Verify logos on the thank-you slide and the shared swag table setup.

docs.title: Post-Conference
docs.text:
• Thank-you email to every sponsor within the first week.
  • Confirm every contracted benefit was delivered; note misses.
  • Feed registration intake demographics to next year's prospectus.
  • Renewal touch 1-2 months later with next year's dates.

docs.title: Swag Runbook
docs.text:
Swag ordering is owned by the Venue Committee. Marketing runs the campaigns around it, including the shirt pre-order last-chance push.

See marketing-committee-runbook.md and venue-committee-runbook.md.

docs.title: What Swag Is
docs.text:
• Shirts: a paid pre-order add-on sold alongside tickets on Pretix, with free-shirt comp classes (speakers, organizers, sponsor allotments).
  • Stickers, patches, and enamel pins: the standing small-item line. Anniversary years add a special line (patches, pins, rubber ducks).
  • Speaker gifts: one nicer item per year (past picks: embroidered BBQ aprons, cups, etched map glasses).
  • Badges and lanyards: separate budget lines; the lanyard is usually sponsor-funded.

A shirt does not come with a ticket. Say so plainly in ticket copy and the KBYG; attendee confusion about this recurs every year.

Plan quantities against real capacity: 250 is the sell-out number, stretchable to 275.

docs.title: The Universal-Shirt Question
docs.text: Giving every attendee a shirt comes up regularly and has not been adopted; shirts remain a paid pre-order. Post-event survey responses lean toward wanting a free shirt included. Treat this as an open question for each year's budget discussion, not as current practice.

docs.title: Order Sequencing
docs.text:
1. ~Week -11: ideation docs (shirt ideas, other swag ideas, speaker gift candidates) with supplier links and minimum-order tradeoffs. Commission the shirt design.
  2. ~Week -8: gather vendor quotes. Remind vendors the Foundation's 501(c)(3) status removes sales tax; quotes drop once the vendor applies it.
  3. ~Week -6.5: pay the first order (patches, stickers, pins).
  4. ~Week -5: shirt pre-orders close. Marketing runs a last-chance campaign the week before.
  5. ~Week -4.5: place the shirt order immediately after pre-orders close.
  6. ~Week -2.5: everything ordered and approved.

Hold sponsor-funded items (lanyards) until the sponsor has paid. The whole window is Weeks -11 to -2.5; no swag is ordered in December.

docs.title: Vendors
docs.text:
• Kong Screenprinting (Austin) for shirts and screen printing; quotes come through Printavo.
  • Do not let the vendor alter the logo; print vendors will "improve" it and degrade it if allowed. Require the supplied art as-is unless there is a real production reason.
  • Stickers: the well-known marketplace vendor upcharges; shop alternatives.
  • Badges: ConferenceBadges.com (template, print ahead plus day-of). The badge order tends to slip into the final two weeks; budget and order it earlier than feels necessary.
  • Specialty items: re-quote before committing; asking a second time often turns up a cheaper vendor.

docs.title: Shirts
docs.text:
• Sold as a paid pre-order add-on on Pretix; sizes are collected at purchase for pre-orders, but comp classes, day-of sales, and buffer stock still need a deliberate size estimate. Skimping on buffer sizes means running short on day 1.
  • Comp classes are tracked in the budget sheet.
  • Organizer shirts: a distinct color from attendee shirts, chosen each year. A second distinct style marks the program/speaker team. Collect staff sizes early.
  • Give sponsors a pre-order deadline (~5 weeks out) for guaranteed day-of pickup.
  • Distribution is by poker chip redemption at a staffed shirt table. Chips need pre-sorting or stuffing into badges ahead of time, and that job cannot fall on one person during registration.
  • When sizes run short, stand up a T-shirt waitlist form on day 1.
  • Hand shirts out in paper bags.

docs.title: Day-Of Swag Sales
docs.text:
• Extra swag (anniversary items, prior-year shirts at a discount) sells day-of through Pretix voucher-redemption QR codes, not cash.
  • Generate the QR codes with segno (Python library); publish them in docs posted at the swag table.
  • Set the swag store up ahead of time, not during registration.

docs.title: Post-Conference
docs.text:
• Count leftovers by item and size for next year's planning
  • Store leftovers for meetups and community events
  • Note vendor performance in the retro

docs.title: Ideas Worth Pursuing
docs.text:
• Get a badge sponsor; consider programmable badges (they run MicroPython).
  • Hand out beanies or similar at PyCon with a CFP-and-tickets card inside.

docs.title: Venue Committee Runbook
docs.text:
Responsibilities: venue relationship and contract logistics, A/V vendor, catering and food service, evening events, alcohol compliance (TABC permit and peace officers), swag ordering, badges, linens, signage, registration desk day-of, volunteers.

See venue.md, av.md, catering.md, network-event.md, volunteers.md, day-of-operations-guide.md, day-of-supplies.md.

docs.title: Month -13 to -12: Venue Contract
docs.text:
Next year's venue contract is signed immediately after the current conference; the Conference Chair leads this with Venue Committee support. See venue.md for contract mechanics and next-year-planning.md for the workstream.

  • Review this year's venue experience (what worked, capacity, pricing, acoustics)
  • Conflict-check candidate dates against the Austin events spreadsheet (Easter, Passover, Texas Relays, Cap10k, SXSW proximity, graduations)
  • Sign the facility use agreement and pay the 50% deposit at signing
  • Document the rationale for next year

docs.title: Month -7 to -3: A/V Vendor
docs.text:
See av.md for the deep dive.

  • Month -7: start vendor outreach (current vendor: Garner Media)
  • Month -6 to -5.5: request the quote; confirm scope covers recording, livestream, and captioning
  • Review the contract and sign with Conference Chair signoff
  • Pay the deposit; coordinate the schedule with Finance (deposit at booking, installment near the event, final after)

docs.title: Month -5.5: Ticket Timeline and Registration Setup
docs.text:
• Set the ticket timeline with Finance: early bird opens Dec 1, speaker list ~week of Jan 7, early bird closes mid-January
  • Start Pretix setup, including demographic questions
  • Configure shirts as a pre-order add-on alongside tickets

docs.title: Month -4 to -3: Alcohol Compliance Starts
docs.text:
Any alcohol service needs a TABC permit and two hired licensed peace officers (a city requirement; two are budgeted). Both are long-lead and fragile. Peace officer hiring can take a month of bounced emails and often closes through a personal contact. TABC approval is slow; a permit submitted a few weeks out can still be in review the day before the conference.

  • Start peace officer outreach now; expect bounced contacts and dead ends
  • Identify the TABC permit requirements and application lead time
  • Agree on the worst case with the Chair in advance ("worst case no alcohol")

docs.title: Week -11 to -8: Catering and Swag Ideation
docs.text:
See catering.md.

  • Build the catering ideas doc with headcount assumptions (~50-75 Friday dinner, ~150 Saturday network event)
  • Build swag ideation docs (shirt ideas, other swag, speaker gifts)
  • Gather catering, bartending, and swag quotes (~8-10 weeks out); remind vendors the 501(c)(3) status removes sales tax
  • Week -8.5: confirm catering deposits and headcounts (deposits roughly half of totals)
  • Book the network event venue (see network-event.md)

docs.title: Week -6.5 to -4.5: Orders and Plans
docs.text:
• Build the catering plan sheet (~6 weeks out): per-day blocks (breakfast, coffee, snacks, all-day beverages) plus a "who's getting what" shopping tab with an owner per item
  • Pay the first swag order (patches, stickers, pins) ~6.5 weeks out
  • Pay both dinner-venue deposits
  • Close shirt pre-orders ~5 weeks out (Marketing runs the last-chance campaign); place the shirt order immediately after
  • Final catering orders due ~4.5 weeks out
  • Order linens from American Party Rental (the library provides none; reuse last year's invoice)
  • Confirm the peace officers are secured
  • Start collecting dietary restrictions from registration; collecting them in the final week is too late
  • Order badges from ConferenceBadges.com (template, print ahead plus day-of printing). Badge orders tend to slip to the final two weeks; order them here and beat the pattern

docs.title: Week -3.5 to -2.5: Compliance and Final Swag
docs.text:
• Submit the TABC permit if not already in (see the warning above; this is the last responsible moment, not the target)
  • All swag ordered and approved
  • Finalize both dinner plans
  • Raise the hotel room block question with the Chair and get a decision; this question tends to drift unresolved

docs.title: Week -2 to -1: Signage and Final Prep
docs.text:
• Plan signage on a Miro board: ~6 standing signs, 5-10 single-page; check whether the library owns sign holders
  • Print signage
  • Confirm venue access times (Friday-Sunday, 6:00 AM to 7:00 PM; there is no Thursday access)
  • Ask the library for reserved organizer parking (the parking attendant said reserving is routine)
  • Pre-conference walkthrough with the venue contact
  • Final head counts to caterers; write down each year's delivery windows (breakfast before doors, afternoon during the mid-afternoon break)
  • Decide the leftover-food policy in advance (standing policy: give to library staff)
  • Confirm A/V on-site hours all 3 days
  • Gather supplies and emergency kit (see day-of-supplies.md)
  • Confirm dietary restrictions are collected for the Friday dinner and checked for Saturday

docs.title: Registration Desk and Volunteers
docs.text:
See registration.md and volunteers.md.

  • Plan the three-station flow: check-in, badge pickup, shirt pickup by poker chip
  • 2 on check-in laptops, 1-2 on badges; lanyards on a stand separate from badges; 3-table bubble layout leaves room for backpacks
  • Test check-in end-to-end
  • Plan edge cases: name not in system, late add, sponsor/comp tickets, day-2 badge loss (stock blank badges plus a label printer and loaner lanyards)
  • Recruit volunteers via email, social, prior years, student orgs; 2-3 hour shifts with coverage plus backup
  • Brief volunteers before doors; give them an identifier (shirt or badge)

The registration bot fails on corporate bulk purchases (registering email vs attendee email); have a manual override ready.

docs.title: Conference Days
docs.text:
See day-of-operations-guide.md for the full run of day. Setup happens Friday morning in parallel with tutorials; there is no Thursday access.

  • Photograph venue property at load-in (and again at load-out) to avoid damage disputes
  • Friday: 6:00 AM venue access, then coffee pickup and registration, food, and linens setup before doors; Costco + HEB supply run during the morning tutorial
  • Reg desk set before doors on Saturday and Sunday
  • Catering deliveries before doors; tear down food after each window (food out for an hour is food gone)
  • Two food lines, clearly marked; people miss the second one, so sign it or post a volunteer
  • Lunch: post the restaurant map on a slide before dismissal; captains with flags lead groups
  • Each evening: pack leftovers (to library staff), secure equipment, brief the next day

docs.title: Week 1
docs.text:
• Return equipment (photograph condition)
  • Process final vendor invoices with Finance
  • Thank volunteers, venue staff, A/V, caterers

docs.title: Vendor Evaluation
docs.text:
• A/V: equipment, support, responsiveness, value, use again?
  • Catering: food quality, dietary handling, timing, value, use again?
  • Venue: space, staff, value, issues, use again?
  • Document for next year

docs.title: Retrospective
docs.text:
• Committee retro: what worked, what didn't, action items
  • Update this runbook
  • Update the vendor contact list with notes
  • Update catering quantities from counted leftovers
  • Archive setup photos

docs.title: Food Quantity Calibration
docs.text:
Count leftovers every year and adjust.

  • Bananas: budget about one per two to three attendees per day (about 40-50 lb at full capacity)
  • Diet and zero sodas, sparkling water, and fruit are the hits
  • Muffins and kolaches tend to be over-ordered; order fewer
  • Buy light on Friday to gauge preferences, then bulk for the weekend
  • Order ice online; store runs are the fallback restock and eat organizer time
  • Coffee is the largest catering friction and budget overrun

See catering.md for the full plan-sheet structure.

docs.title: Cross-Committee
docs.text:
• Conference: operations updates, escalations, major decisions
  • Marketing: signage, shirt last-chance campaign, swag distribution
  • Speaker: A/V needs, tech checks, timing
  • Finance: vendor payments, headcounts, budget tracking, insurance deadline (Week -4.5)
  • Community: registration data, attendee comms, volunteer recruitment

docs.title: Emergency Procedures
docs.text:
These are untested defaults, not procedures proven at a past conference. The venue's own emergency procedures come first; escalate to the Conference Chair.

Medical:

  • Call 911, notify the Conference Chair
  • Provide assistance if trained
  • Have someone meet EMTs at the entrance
  • Document

Fire or evacuation:

  • Follow venue procedures
  • Announce calmly, direct to exits
  • Account for organizers
  • Don't re-enter until cleared

Catering no-show:

  • Notify the Conference Chair
  • Emergency Costco or grocery run
  • Communicate the delay

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Poker chips for shirt distribution work but need pre-sorting or chips placed inside badges; keep the shirt table staffed; say loudly whether a shirt comes with the ticket.
  • Do not let the print vendor alter the logo.
  • Coffee runs over budget every year; it is the largest catering friction.
  • Food out for an hour is food gone, except the forbidden item of the year.
  • Hallway echo is loud enough to ring heads; sound deadening is an open problem.
  • Power strips at every tutorial table; missing power is a recurring complaint.
  • Tech checks are Friday (before 9:00 or at lunch), not a separate setup day.
  • The phone-numbers roster in the Org Info Sheet beats chat in emergencies.

docs.title: Venue Runbook
docs.text:
Owned by Venue Committee.

See venue-committee-runbook.md for the full operations workflow and av.md for A/V vendor details.

docs.title: Current Venue: Austin Central Library
docs.text: Address: 710 W Cesar Chavez St, Austin, TX 78701 Map: library.austintexas.gov/node/1734558

docs.title: Spaces
docs.text:
Special Event Center (main, 1st floor): - 4,450 sq ft; 250 is the sell-out number, stretchable to 275; theater max 350 - Use: talks, keynotes; Pre-Function Area for registration and sponsor tables - Green room, private restrooms - Library provides furniture but no linens (rent from American Party Rental)

Access hours: - 6:00 AM to 7:00 PM, Friday through Sunday - There is no Thursday access; setup happens Friday morning in parallel with tutorials

Rooftop Garden: - Evening hours (6:00 PM to midnight) - Not part of the standard booking; the evening events default to off-site venues (see network-event.md) - Running rooftop events adds logistics burden (equipment security, after-hours access, weather backup); book it only with a strong reason

Kitchen: - Cold storage available - No full cooking facilities - Catering brought in - Coordinate access with vendor

First floor demo space: - Billed hourly with a 2-hour minimum - Not part of the standard booking; the demo area never sells out as a sponsor add-on, so skip it

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Assess and budget for equipment security whenever the rooftop is used, and confirm after-hours access rules with the library. Equipment includes A/V, sponsor materials, and supplies.

docs.title: Date Selection
docs.text: Dates are chosen by conflict-checking a spreadsheet of Austin events: Easter, Passover, Texas Relays, Cap10k, the kite festival, SXSW proximity, graduations. The Chair runs this ~11 weeks before the current conference so next year's contract can be signed right after it. See next-year-planning.md.

docs.title: Contract Mechanics
docs.text:
• Nonprofit composite hourly rate; the contract covers three 13-hour days (6:00 AM to 7:00 PM)
  • 50% deposit at signing, with a 14-day deadline to return the signed agreement
  • Balance due about 3 months before the event (Jan 10-11 for an April conference)
  • Cancellation tiers at 91+ days, 31-90 days, and 30 days
  • Insurance certificate and A/V-vendor coordination required; the library emails about this ~2 months out
  • File amendments (space or hours changes) as soon as space or hours change; do not sit on them
  • Library pricing may rise year over year; get the next-year contract signed by February 1

docs.title: 12+ Months Out
docs.text:
Sign next year's facility use agreement immediately after the current conference and pay the deposit.

Selection criteria if considering a move: - Capacity for 250-275 (the current sell-out range; 350 theater max at the library) - Accessible (transit, parking) - A/V or vendor support - Food service options - Within budget (hotel routes have failed on room-block risk and F&B minimums) - Mid-April dates available

docs.title: 6-8 Months Out
docs.text:
• Confirm dates and spaces
  • Amendment if space or hours change
  • Insurance requirements
  • Load-in/out times
  • Venue restrictions (signage, food, decorations)

docs.title: 3-4 Months Out
docs.text:
• Tour with committee leads
  • Plan layouts and capacity
  • Reg desk location
  • Sponsor booth/table locations
  • Signage placement
  • Coordinate with A/V vendor

docs.title: 1-2 Months Out
docs.text:
• Final room setup confirmed

docs.text: Day-of staffing defaults to organizers plus whoever's free. That barely works at 250 attendees and leaves no slack for rotations or breaks. Without a published intake form, people walk up at registration asking how to volunteer and a form gets built mid-conference.

docs.text: • CFP Review

docs.title: Review of new submissions to CFP
docs.text:
Congratulations, someone has submitted to the Call For Proposals (CFP). Here's what to do.

  1. Look at the submission and ask the following questions. If you have any questions or doubts about any of these, talk about it in the #organizers-text Discord channel.
    • Is this topic a good fit fot the meetup audience? Talks for the meetup probably should have some sort of wide appeal, and definitely MUST follow the code of conduct guidelines.
    • Does it feel like this topic could be adequately covered in 30-60 minutes? Talks shorter than 30 minutes might need to be combined with another shorter talk to make a sufficient meetup out of. Talks longer than 60 minutes run the risk of a lot of attendence drop-off.
    • Does the submission give you the impression that the speaker can cover the topic? This might be very hard from to tell from just the submission, but if you have any concern, it may be a good idea to reach out to the speaker with some questions.
    • Does the submission feel like its goal is advertise a paid product? If so, we may not want to approve it. The dividing line comes down to the "primary purpose" of the talk. If it feels like the main goal is to illustrate some language feature, technique, pattern, library, or something else; and happens to use a paid product, then it is probably fine. If it feels like the focus of the talk is the paid product, then it is probably not fine.
  2. Assuming the talk has not been rejected, identify a month for the speaker to present in.
  3. Contact the speaker and confirm that they are available to speak during the selected month. Have them fill out the Speaker Intake Form (in the meetup Drive folder).

When the speaker's month arrives, update the PyTexas Meetup website with the information.

docs.title: Create Run of Show Document
docs.text: The run of show document lists off the initerary for the PyTexas meetup. This document should be produced before the meetup, updated up to the day of the meetup, and followed to ensure a successful meetup.

docs.title: What you will need
docs.text:
• Access to the PyTexas 1Password
  • Access to the PyTexas Meetup Google Drive

docs.title: Create the Slido
docs.text:
1. Go to slido.com and choose "Login".
  2. Login using the PyTexas username and password from 1Password.
  3. Click "Create Slido".
  4. In the dialog that appears, set the dates to the date of the meetup, and for the name, use PyTexas <month> <year> Meetup, where <month> is the month name (like "July" or "August") and <year> is the 4-digit year (such as "2024"). Once done, click "Create Slido".
  5. If you want to create any polls so that they can be used on the day of, you can use the options present.
  6. Click on "Share" and choose "Share link with participants". This will copy the link to the Slido to the clipboard. Save this to paste into the Run of Show document.

docs.title: Create the Attendance Survey
docs.text:
1. Go to Google Drive and login.
  2. Navigate to the "PyTexas Meetup" shared drive, and the "Meetups" subfolder.
  3. Navigate to the subfolder for the meetup date. If a folder does not exist, create a new one with a namein the form of YYYY-MM-DD (example: 2024-07-02), and navigate to it.
  4. Create a new Google Forms document. This will open the document.
  5. Set the follwoing content:
  6. Title: PyTexas Virtual Meetup Attendance <YYYY-MM-DD> where <YYYY-MM-DD> is the date of the meetup
  7. Description: 
    Thank you for filling out this quick attendance form. Your information will not be shared with anyone, this is just 
for our metrics.

By filling out this form you are entered in a door prize drawing at the end of the meetup! (You must be present to 
win).
  8. Add the following questions:
  9. Name (Short Answer, required)
  10. Are you currently a resident of Texas? (Multiple Choice, required)
    • Yes, Currently
    • Not presently
    • No
  11. If so, what major city/region do you live closest to? (Multiple Choice)
    • Austin
    • College Station
    • Dallas/Fort Worth
    • El Paso
    • Houston
    • Lubbock
    • Rio Grande Valley
    • San Antonio
  12. In the "Settings" tab, expand "Responses" and ensure "Restrict to users in PyTexas Foundation and its trusted organizations" is turned off.
  13. Click "Send", choose the "Link" tab, click the "Shorten URL" checkbox and click the "Copy" button. This will copy the link to the survey to the clipboard. Save this to paste into the Run of Show document.

docs.title: Create the Run of Show document
docs.text:
1. Go to Google Drive and login.
  2. Navigate to the "PyTexas Meetup" shared drive, and the "Meetups" subfolder.
  3. Navigate to the subfolder for the meetup date. If a folder does not exist, create a new one with a namein the form of YYYY-MM-DD (example: 2024-07-02), and navigate to it.
  4. Either copy a Run of Show document from a previous meetup and update the content, or create a new document and follow a similar flow. Each run of show document should contain the following sections:
  5. Schedule - This should contain the schedule of events for the meetup day, including the AV check, pre-meetup chat, meetup events, and post-meetup chat.
  6. Roles - This should contain a list of organizer roles and who is fulfilling what. Currently this includes the hosts and moderators (aka backstage).

  7. Announcements - This should contain a list of announcements that we want to cover at the beginning of the meetup. Announcements are usually for things going on around the community, such as the PyTexas Conference, other regional conferences, or other featured happenings.

    This should also contain the links to the Slido and Attendance Survey created in the previous 2 sections. * Speaker - This should contain the speaker name, talk title, and description from the CFP document. This can contain additional information from the speaker that can be used to introduce them. * Upcoming Meetups - This should contain the dates, locations, and names of upcoming local meetups occurring within the Texas area. Use the Meetup site's Local Meetups page and the local channels in Discord to dig these up. * Next Month - This should contain the speaker name, talk title, and description for the next month's meetup, so that we can tease it. * Drawing Winner - This space will be reserved to fill in the drawing winner, so we can keep track of this. 5. Save the document, and get a share link. Share the link to the document in the #organizers-text channel.

docs.title: Meetup Night-of Workflow
docs.text: A lot goes into facilitating the meetup. Here are the various activities that occur on the day of.

docs.title: What you will need
docs.text:
• Access to the PyTexas Meetup Google Drive
  • PyTexas Meetup Organizer role in Discord.

docs.title: More than an hour before the meetup
docs.text:
• Confirm with the other organizers who is performing what role. While the meetup can be run with a single host only, we prefer to have 1-2 hosts (so that there can be banter), and 1-3 backstage.
  • Check the run-of-show document and ensure that the upcoming community meetup information is complete and accurate.
  • Ensure that the speaker is confirmed to be available an hour before the meetup for an AV check.

docs.title: An hour before the meetup
docs.text:
• Start the test stage and meet with the speaker for AV check. It is encouraged that any available host and backstage staff attend. During the AV check, the following things should check:
  • Check that the the speaker is audible.
  • Check that the speaker is able to share video.
  • Check that the speaker is able to share their content.
  • Check that the speaker is familiar with the Discord UI, and know how to access the chat and share options.
  • Check that the hosts and backstage have links and access to the content, as a backup.
  • Talk the speaker through the run of show and answer any questions.
  • Get any preferences that the speaker has on how questions and feedback will be delivered.
  • Capture how the speaker would like to be introduced, including name pronounciation, preferred gender, and bio.

docs.title: Thirty minutes before the meetup
docs.text:
• Start up the chat in the meetup-discussions audio channel.
  • Post to the announcements channel with an @everyone tag to say that the meetup is starting in 30 minutes and that the meetup pre-chat has begun.
  • Keep the chat going. Ensure we welcome anyone who joins, and encourage them to join in as they wish.

docs.title: At meetup start
docs.text:
• Start the event in Discord, which should open the stage and send a message with @everyone.
  • Follow the run of show document

docs.title: After the meetup
docs.text: • Start up the chat in the meetup-discussions audio channel.
